Family Name: Principles for voluntary carbon and nature market integrity
Family Summary:
The UK government principles for voluntary carbon and nature market integrity are:

1. Use credits in addition to ambitious actions within value chains;

2. Use high integrity credits;

3. Measure and disclose the planned use of credits as part of sustainability reporting;

4. Plan ahead;

5. Make accurate green claims using appropriate terminology; and

6. Co-operate with others to support the growth of high integrity markets.
Document Title: Principles for voluntary carbon and nature market integrity

Family Name: Supreme Decree No. 010-2024-MINAM. Supreme Decree on the operation of the National Registry of Mitigation Measures (RENAMI) [Decreto Supremo N° 010-2024-MINAM. Decreto Supremo sobre el funcionamiento del Registro Nacional de Medidas de Mitigación (RENAMI)]
Family Summary: This Peruvian Supreme Decree establishes operational provisions for the National Registry of Mitigation Measures (RENAMI), a measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) tool administered by the Ministry of Environment through its Directorate General of Climate Change and Desertification. The registry comprises three components: mitigation measures forming Peru's Nationally Determined Contribution (declarative nature), carbon market mitigation measures under cooperative approaches and their emission reduction units (constitutive nature), and voluntary carbon market mitigation measures (declarative nature). The instrument delineates institutional responsibilities, with the Ministry managing registrations, recognising certification standards and methodologies, authorising international transfers of emission reduction units as Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs), and maintaining the national GHG emissions balance. Sectoral authorities must report monitoring data for NDC measures under their responsibility and provide technical opinions on carbon market projects. The decree establishes that carbon market measures under cooperative approaches, implemented through Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, generate emission reduction units eligible for international transfer to meet other countries' NDCs or international mitigation purposes such as CORSIA, whilst voluntary carbon market measures may contribute to Peru's NDC implementation within corresponding emission sectors.
Document Title: Supreme Decree No. 010-2024-MINAM. Supreme Decree approving the provisions for the operation of the National Registry of Mitigation Measures (RENAMI) [Decreto Supremo No. 010-2024-MINAM. Decreto Supremo que aprueba las disposiciones para el funcionamiento del Registro Nacional de Medidas de Mitigación (RENAMI)]

Family Name: Methodological Guide for the Consideration of Climate Change in the Environmental Impact Assessment System
Family Summary: Issued by Chile's Environmental Assessment Service (SEA) in November 2024, this document is the third edition of the Methodological Guide for the Consideration of Climate Change in the Environmental Impact Assessment System (SEIA). Its publication was made necessary by Supreme Decree No. 30 of 2023, which amended the SEIA Regulations and formally mandated the incorporation of the climate change variable into the environmental assessment procedure. The Guide requires that project proponents integrate climate change considerations throughout all stages of Environmental Impact Statements and Assessments. For example, baseline descriptions must incorporate the adverse effects of climate change and impact prediction must account for the variability of environmental elements as a result of climate change.
Document Title: Methodological Guide

Family Name: Order No. 13808/2024 (appoints the representatives of the VCM technical monitoring committee)
Family Summary: This Order appoints the representatives of the VCM technical monitoring committee provided for in Decree Law No. 4/2024. The representatives are from various government environmental and energy agencies, and experts in climate change and economics.
Document Title: Order No. 13808/2024 (appoints the representatives of the VCM technical monitoring committee)

Family Name: Fiji National Carbon Market Strategy Roadmap
Family Summary:
This Strategy Roadmap provides an important overview of carbon market options, opportunities, risks, and priority actions which will help guide further policy development in Fiji and provides a basis for its interactions with new market-based opportunities. Carbon markets are meant to be an additional means to increase investment in sustainable development.

It is designed for use by policymakers, project developers, investors, land and resource owners, credit buyers, local communities, and other relevant stakeholders to shape their potential interaction with carbon market mechanisms.

It contains five chapters:

  • Chapter 1: A market vision, priorities and principles co-designed with multi- stakeholders.
  • Chapter 2: Fiji’s NDC targets, existing financing options, potential roles for high-integrity carbon markets, and the current state of play of carbon projects.
  • Chapter 3: Opportunities and risks, both general and specific to Fiji’s local contexts.
  • Chapter 4: Strategic considerations and options for engagement with carbon markets.
  • Chapter 5: Key pillar action items to enhance market readiness in Fiji, encompassing legal, governance, community benefits and landowner rights, partnerships, and finance.
Document Title: Fiji National Carbon Market Strategy Roadmap

Collection Name: The Mother Earth Law and Integral Development to Live Well, Framework Law No 300
Collection Summary:
The Mother Earth Law is a piece of legislation that epitomises Bolivia's dedication to sustainable development, respecting the balance between human life and the natural environment, and prioritising the rights and knowledge of the country's majority indigenous population. The expressed objective of the law is to 'establish the vision and fundamentals of integral development in harmony and balance with Mother Earth to Live Well, guaranteeing the continued capacity of Mother Earth to regenerate natural systems, recuperating and strengthening local and ancestral practices, within the framework of rights, obligations and responsibilities'.
 
 In relation to climate change the law has many provisions that outline the state's vision, citizens' rights, and responsibilities. It embraces the concept of 'climate justice', defined by the ability of all Bolivian citizens to 'Live Well', especially those who are most vulnerable to climate change. It reinforces the point that some states have more of a global responsibility to respond to climate change.
 
 To encourage sustainable development of natural resources, it states that climate change trajectories should be accounted for when planning and zoning responsible land use.
 
 The law focuses on reducing the risks posed by climate change through six lines of actions:
The permanent incorporation of prevention of and managed response to natural disasters into the System of Integral Planning
Risk management for the agricultural sector to prevent diminished crop yields and food insecurity
The adoption of risk management of disasters as well as adaption to climate change across state development projects; development of informational networks to issue early warnings in times of natural crisis as well as to assist the agricultural industry and indigenous communities plan according to climate conditions
Strengthening territorial management processes of sub-national governments through the incorporation of risk management and adaption to climate change perspectives
Articulation between public and private scientific research sectors to share knowledge and co-ordinate research regarding vulnerabilities related to climate change
 
 The Law defines 'Living Well' in relation to climate change and lays out the state's legal obligations. The state will develop policies, strategies and legal techniques to mitigate the effects of climate change and adapt to them through strengthening institutional capacities for the monitoring of climate with the purpose of long-term planning. The state will also encourage the recuperation of traditional indigenous practices that were historically sustainable and allowed for the natural regeneration of resources.
 
 The law also establishes the Plurinational Authority of Mother Earth, within the Ministry of Environment and Water, as the state entity responsible for much of the development, overseeing and co-ordination of projects, programmes and research as it relates to climate change and the objectives of the Plurinational Plan for Climate Change. It also co-ordinates scientific monitoring of GHG emissions. The entity will operate within the framework of 'climate justice,' following the principles of Bolivia's climate change politics.
 
 The Authority will operate through three mechanisms: (1) Joint Mechanism of Mitigation and Adaptation for the Integral and Sustainable Management of Mother Earth's Forests; (2) Mitigation Mechanism to 'Living Well'; and (3) Adaptation Mechanism to 'Living Well'.
 
 The Authority is also responsible for the management of the Plurinational Fund of Mother Earth. The Fund will be financed with multilateral and bilateral aid, public money from the national government allocated to mitigation or adaptation, funds from private donors, national or international loans, and funds at the disposal of the executive branch.
Family Name: Supreme Decree 5264, establishing the climate finance management and access guidelines for implementing Bolivia's Nationally Determined Contributions
Family Summary: The Bolivia Supreme Decree 5264 establishes a comprehensive framework for climate finance management and access, supporting the implementation of Bolivia's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). Building upon Law 300 (Framework Law of Mother Earth and Integral Development for Living Well), this Supreme Decree emphasises the Bolivian vision for a development in harmony with Mother Earth for the living-well (Vivir-Bien), protecting both Mother Earth's rights and the rights of indigenous-peasant communities, particularly concerning climate crisis context.The Supreme Decree creates an institutional structure that distributes responsibilities across different ministries and establishes the National Registry of Programs and Projects (RENAPP) for tracking climate initiatives and emission reduction units. The decree assigns specific roles to key ministries: (1) evaluation and prioritisation of projects by the Ministries of Hydrocarbons and Energy, Environment and Water, and Rural Development; (2) management of RENAPP by the Ministry of Environment and Water; (3) oversight of debt-for-nature swaps and carbon credits by the Ministry of Economy and Public Finance; (4) access to climate finance mechanisms by the Ministry of Development Planning.Equally, this Supreme Decree establishes four fundamental guiding principles for climate finance: (1) Sovereignty, ensuring state control over natural resources and emission reduction units; (2) Transparency, requiring mandatory disclosure of climate finance information; (3) Common but Differentiated Responsibilities, aligning with UNFCCC and Paris Agreement principles; (4) Precautionary Principle, emphasising preventive measures for environmental protection.Moreover, the scope of the Supreme Decree encompasses public entities, state-owned enterprises, and private actors (both domestic and foreign), applying to both national and subnational climate change mitigation and adaptation projects.
Document Title: Supreme Decree 5264, establishing the climate finance management and access guidelines for implementing Bolivia's Nationally Determined Contributions

Family Name: Alignment of Mexico's National Biodiversity Strategy and 2030 Action Plan with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework Targets (Alineación de la Estrategia Nacional sobre Biodiversidad de México y Plan de Acción 2030 con las Metas del Marco Mundial de Biodiversidad de Kunming-Montreal)
Family Summary: Mexico began aligning its National Biodiversity Strategy (ENBioMex) with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework through a national process led by CONABIO. As a result, the Alignment of Mexico's National Biodiversity Strategy (ENBioMex) and 2030 Action Plan with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) Targets recognises climate change as a critical driver of biodiversity loss, embedding it explicitly in Target 8, which calls for minimising climate and ocean acidification impacts on biodiversity through mitigation, adaptation, and disaster risk reduction. Other targets promote ecosystem-based approaches and nature-based solutions that bolster biodiversity’s role in climate resilience, reinforcing the interdependence of global climate and biodiversity goals.
Document Title: Alignment of Mexico's National Biodiversity Strategy and 2030 Action Plan with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework Targets (Alineación de la Estrategia Nacional sobre Biodiversidad de México y Plan de Acción 2030 con las Metas del Marco Mundial de Biodiversidad de Kunming-Montreal)

Family Name: Supreme Decree No. 203-2024-EF, approving the update of the National Competitiveness and Productivity Plan 2019-2030 (Decreto Supremo No. 203-2024-EF, que aprueba la actualización del Plan Nacional de Competitividad y productividad 2019-2030
Family Summary: The Supreme Decree No. 203-2024-EF updates Peru’s National Competitiveness and Productivity Plan (PNCP 2024–2030), embedding climate finance and monitoring mechanisms into its ninth strategic objective, “Promote environmental sustainability in economic activities.” This includes Policy Measure 9.1 (“Climate Finance and Monitoring”), which addresses institutional barriers to accessing international climate funds (e.g., the Green Climate Fund) and integrates climate considerations into financial decision-making. The plan mandates the implementation of a Sistema de Monitoreo to track adaptation/mitigation progress, emissions reductions, and funding flows. This system comprises three components: (i) measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) of greenhouse gas emissions/removals; (ii) monitoring and evaluation (ME) of adaptation measures; and (iii) tracking of climate finance allocation. The policy aligns Peru’s climate action with international obligations under the Paris Agreement and SDG 13, prioritising capacity-building for public and private actors to access climate financing. It recognises the fiscal urgency of adaptation, citing a projected PEN 66 billion cost for 51 adaptation measures by 2030 (per MINAM’s 2021 National Adaptation Plan).
Document Title: Supreme Decree No. 203-2024-EF updates Peru’s National Competitiveness and Productivity Plan (PNCP 2024–2030)

Family Name: National Strategy for Biological Diversity to 2050 (Estrategia Nacional de Diversidad Biológica al 2050)
Family Summary: Peru’s National Strategy for Biological Diversity to 2050 establishes a long-term framework to address biodiversity loss through integrated, participatory governance aligned with climate resilience and sustainable development. Central to the strategy are five strategic objectives targeting land-use change, climate impacts, pollution, invasive species, and institutional weaknesses. These objectives operationalise principles such as the precautionary principle (Rio Declaration, Principle 15), intercultural equity, and human rights-based approaches, ensuring alignment with international obligations under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and the Paris Agreement. The strategy mandates ecosystem-based adaptation, including restoring 10% of degraded ecosystems and species affected by climate change, while integrating traditional ecological knowledge to strengthen adaptive capacity. The strategy’s implementation relies on institutional reforms, such as strengthening multi-level governance and integrating biodiversity metrics (e.g., the Lista Roja de Ecosistemas) into national reporting frameworks, including the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. It addresses climate-biodiversity linkages by prioritising mitigation of climate-driven threats (e.g., deforestation, water pollution) and promoting nature-based solutions, such as community-led water harvesting projects. The "Enfoque Territorial" (territorial approach) ensures localised, context-specific actions, while the Enfoque "Una Salud" (One Health) links ecosystem health to human and animal well-being.
Document Title: National Biological Diversity Strategy to 2050 (Estrategia Nacional de Diversidad Biológica al 2050)

Family Name: Agricultural Sector Mitigation Plan
Family Summary: This plan outlines the mitigation measures needed for Chile’s agriculture, livestock, and forestry sector to meet its NDC and other sectoral targets, particularly supporting the AFOLU sector's role as a net carbon sink contributing to Chile's 2050 climate neutrality goal.
Document Title: Agricultural Sector Mitigation Plan (Plan Sectorial de Mitigación al Cambio Climático - Sector Agricultura)

Family Name: National Climate Security Strategy 2024-2028
Family Summary: National Climate Security Strategy 2024-2028 aims to address the significant climate adaptation needs of Burkina Faso, up to 2028 and in the longer term. The strategy operates along four strategic axes: improving climate security governance; sustainable and climate-just management of natural resources; improving human protection against disaster risks and crises; improving Burkina Faso's access to climate finance. It primarily outlines gaps in the existing strategic framework, and broader key areas for increased focus, but promotes some specific interventions such as reforestation and the creation of improved natural disaster early warning systems.
Document Title: National Climate Security Strategy 2024-2028

Family Name: Gender Action Plan 2024-2030
Family Summary: The NDC GAP 2024-2030 sets out strategic actions as guidelines for gender-responsive implementation of the current NDC across all mitigation and adaptation policies and measures, primarily in the agriculture, transport, energy, and waste sectors, and industrial processes and product use. It provides both analytical frameworks and proposed entry points for gender mainstreaming. As a product of interagency collaboration and partnership, it highlights opportunities to mainstream the gender and climate nexus in programs and investments to address vulnerabilities and empower marginalised communities.
Document Title: Gender Action Plan 2024-2030

Family Name: PLANAVEG National Native Vegetation Recovery Plan 2025-2028
Family Summary: The "PLANAVEG National Native Vegetation Recovery Plan 2025-2028" was adopted following its renewal at COP16 in October 2024 and aims to restore 12 million hectares of native vegetation in Brazil by 2030. The plan focuses on expanding and strengthening public policies, investment, and coordination among federal, state, and private actors to achieve this restoration target, particularly in compliance with Brazil’s environmental laws and international biodiversity commitments.
Document Title: PLANAVEG National Native Vegetation Recovery Plan

Family Name: Norwegian Action Plan for Biodiversity (Meld. St. 35 2023-2024)
Family Summary:
This Action Plan shows how the government's policy will contribute to the sustainable use and conservation of natural diversity. The measures are meant to ensure that society's use of nature occurs in a way that makes it possible to use nature and live good lives throughout the country in the future.

The proposals in this action plan will, as far as possible, safeguard the interests of both nature and climate, and measures under all 23 goals (of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework) can contribute to development that both preserves natural diversity, reduces greenhouse gas emissions and strengthens society and nature's ability to withstand climate change. In some cases, however, climate and nature considerations will conflict with each other, for example, to the development of renewable energy and the transmission of such energy through power grids and to the extraction of minerals and the establishment of industry that are important for the green shift, as this requires land. The government addresses these issues but emphasises that trade-offs between climate and nature must be made in the ongoing political work of every government.
Document Title: Norwegian Action Plan for Biodiversity (Meld. St. 35 2023-2024)

Family Name: Spain Updated Final National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP). 2021-2030
Family Summary:
The National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) is a ten-year integrated document mandated by the European Union to each of its member states in order for the EU to meet its overall greenhouse gases emissions targets. Following feedback from an EU-wide assessment of draft NECP submissions, EU members are required to submit updated final NECPs for the period 2021-2030. The Energy and Climate Plan addresses all five dimensions of the EU Energy Union: decarbonisation, energy efficiency, energy security, internal energy markets and research, innovation and competitiveness.

The plan sets out the following objectives: 1) to become a carbon-neutral country by 2050 by decreasing the gross total GHG emissions in the electricity, transport, industry sectors ; 2) to promote energy efficiency thanks to the penetration of renewable energy in final energy consumption, efficiency measures to the transport, industry and building sectors, energy saving targets; 3) to ensure energy security by the diversification of the national energy mix, the use of domestic sources and an increase in the flexibility of the national energy system; 4) interconnectivity, energy transmission infrastructure, integration of the internal energy market; 5) to strengthen technology transfers, promote public-private partnership and improve business research and innovation. The updated NECP has an enhanced focus on strategic energy independence, with more ambitious targets to reduce external energy dependency from 73% in 2019 to 50% in 2030. Other key aims include a 55% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions in 2030 relative to 2005, and a 81% renewable share of energy production.
Document Title: Spain Updated Final National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP). 2021-2030

Family Name: National Long-Term Development Plan (RPJPN) 2025-2045
Family Summary:
This Plan, approved in Law No. 59 of 2024, outlines efforts to address various aspects of public needs to realise the vision of “Golden Indonesia 2045, a united, sovereign, advanced, and sustainable Indonesia. It serves as a guideline for:

  1. the formulation, monitoring, and review of laws and regulations;
  2. the formulation of the vision, mission, and programs in the candidacy requirements, campaign materials, and debate materials for: a. b. presidential and vice-presidential candidate pairs; and candidate pairs for governor and deputy governor, regent and deputy regent, and mayor and deputy mayor; and
  3. the preparation of master plans, national strategies, roadmaps, or other similar documents related to the elaboration of long-term and medium-term national development planning.

The Plan describes how various regions are affected by climate change, and actions to mitigate and adapt to climate change. Such actions include implementing climate-smart agriculture that is resilient to climate change; rural environmental management, including climate crisis prevention and disaster resilience; and prevention and control of diseases and health issues caused by climate change.
Document Title: National Long-Term Development Plan (RPJPN) 2025-2045

Family Name: Ministerial Resolution No. 00283-2024-MINAM. Guidelines for the reception, administration, and distribution of REDD+ financing in Peru (Resolución Ministerial N°00283-2024-MINAM. Lineamiento para la recepción, administración y distribución del financiamiento REDD+ en el Perú)
Family Summary: This Peruvian ministerial resolution establishes guidelines for the reception, administration and distribution of REDD+ financing across its three phases: preparation, implementation, and results-based payments. The instrument delineates three administrative modalities for managing REDD+ funds: through public entity budgetary allocations subject to the National Public Budget System; via PROFONANPE (the National Fund for State Protected Natural Areas) specifically for funds from the Joint Declaration of Intent with Germany, Norway and the United Kingdom; and through direct donor administration mechanisms such as trusts. The resolution mandates that the Ministry of Environment and donors jointly determine the appropriate modality based on costs, execution timelines and required human resources, with such determination to be formalised in bilateral or multilateral agreements. For results-based payments, the guidelines stipulate that benefit distribution must be equitable, culturally appropriate and participatory, with the Ministry establishing criteria for beneficiary identification in consultation with state and non-state actors, including indigenous peoples, whilst ensuring continued reduction of greenhouse gas emissions from the Land Use, Land-Use Change and Forestry sector.
Document Title: Guidelines for the reception, administration, and distribution of REDD+ financing in Peru (Lineamiento para la recepción, administración y distribución del financimiento REDD+ en el Perú)

Family Name: The list of positive project areas for implementation of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement in Sri Lanka
Family Summary:
In September 2024, the Government of Sri Lanka approved and published a positive list of project areas that are considered for trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The positive list also includes capping the share of emission reductions that can be credited restricted to renewables energy projects. Some types of renewable projects see their emission reductions are capped at 50% and others at 25%. Eligible activities are as follows:

1. Electricity Sector

- Establishment of wind power plants with the assistance of bilateral and multilateral donor agencies and sovereign governments (to the level of 737 MW) - (Maximum 25%)

- Establishment of ground-mounted solar PV with the assistance of bilateral and multilateral donor agencies and sovereign governments (to the level of 1982 MW) - (Maximum 25%)

- Establishment of Offshore Wind Farms (Maximum 50%)

- Establishment of Tidal Energy Farms (Maximum 50%)

- Establishment of Energy Storage Power Facilities such as Hydro Pumped Power Storage (Maximum 50%)

- Establishment of Energy Storage Power Facilities such as Battery Storage in Solar Power Plants (Maximum 50%)

- Electricity Wheeling (50%)

- Demand Side Management programs other than Lighting efficiency improvements (50%)

2. Transport Sector

- Implementation of fuel switch measures focusing on electric mobility and hybrid vehicles (H2)

- Implementation of low-carbon public passenger transport activities, such as Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) and improved rail transportation

- Implementation of rapid transport systems for passenger transport

- Development of new low-carbon transportation infrastructure resulting in fuel savings

3. Industry Sector

- Fuel switch from fossil fuels to renewable energy-based fuels in industrial processes

- Development of Resource-Efficiency Cleaner Production (RECP) practices, including low-carbon technologies and processes

- Introduction of tri-generation* facilities

- Energy efficiency interventions in industries with longer payback periods

4. Forestry Sector

- Restoration and reforestation of terrestrial forests covering various plantations

- Enhancement and expansion of trees outside forests

- Agroforestry on private lands, covering various large and bundled small activities

- Reforestation by the private sector for timber production

- Mangrove restoration subject to the following conditions

a. Restoration of mangroves based on the areas identified by the Department of Forest Conservation and the Department of Wildlife Conservation, which is approximately 2000 ha in extent, will be restored, however, the aforementioned extent would not be considered and allocated for carbon finance and crediting purposes.

b. Apart from the above-mentioned identified areas, any further areas that might be identified based on National Guidelines on Mangrove Restoration in Sri Lanka (2021), and other protocols for blue carbon ecosystem restoration, and approved by the Blue Carbon Task Force, could be considered.

5. Waste Sector

- Deployment of methane abatement technologies in municipal solid waste treatment projects

- Implementation of Waste-to-Energy projects (Incineration, Gasification, Pyrolysis and Plasma)

- Waste dumpsites rehabilitation projects (Avoidance of greenhouse gas emissions in waste dumps/landfills)

- Deployment of Efficient Waste Collection and Transportation Systems and Processes

- Emission Reductions through the Promotion of Recycling Technologies and Process Optimization

6. Agriculture Sector

- Methane emission management from livestock coupled with energy conversion for thermal or electrical generation

- Adoption of innovative technologies in agricultural practices (such as rice cultivation) for GHG emission reductions
Document Title: The list of positive project areas for implementation of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement in Sri Lanka

Family Name: CONPES 4088/2022 - Declaration of strategic importance of investment projects for the implementation of actions that lead to low-carbon and climate-resilient development
Family Summary:
The CONPES 4088 Document of 2022 is an initiative by the Colombian National Government that declares seven investment projects as strategically important to promote low-carbon and climate-resilient development. These projects align with the country's commitments to climate change and aim to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and enhance the resilience of productive sectors and ecosystems in Colombia.

Amidst the projects, there are key points such as the conservation and sustainable use of ecosystems, strengthening of the climate change management in sectoral planning and sustainable agricultural and forestry development.

These projects are set to be developed between 2022 and 2025 and the implementation of these projects is crucial to advancing a sustainable development model that integrates climate change mitigation and the adaptation of the country's productive sectors and ecosystems.
Document Title: CONPES 4088/2022 - Declaration of strategic importance of investment projects for the implementation of actions that lead to low-carbon and climate-resilient development.

Family Summary:

Family Name: Germany Updated Final National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP). 2021-2030
Family Summary:
The National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) is a ten-year integrated document mandated by the European Union to each of its member states in order for the EU to meet its overall greenhouse gases emissions targets. Following feedback from an EU-wide assessment of draft NECP submissions, EU members are required to submit updated final NECPs for the period 2021-2030. . The Energy and Climate Plan addresses all five dimensions of the EU Energy Union: decarbonisation, energy efficiency, energy security, internal energy markets and research, innovation and competitiveness.

The plan provides an overview of the country’s energy and climate policy as well as the current status of plans in these areas. Several measures and strategies are implemented to address the five dimensions of the EU Energy Union: 1) Decarbonisation: implementation of the Climate Action Plan 2050 and the Climate Action Programme 2030, better regionalisation of growth of renewable energies, increase the consumption of self-generated electricity, subsidies for electrically powered vehicles (environmental bonus), etc.; 2) Energy efficiency: energy efficiency strategy for buildings, tax incentives for energy-related building renovations, carbon pricing in the heating and transport sectors, etc.; 3) Energy security: Act on the Security of the Electricity and Gas Supply, national preventive action and emergency plans for natural gas, etc; 4) Internal energy market: promote interconnectivity (regional cooperation), etc.; 5) Research, innovation, competitiveness: greater involvement of start-ups, increased technology transfer. Quantified targets in the plan include at least a 65% reduction in net greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, from a 1990 baseline, and a 42.5% renewabe energy share of gross final consumption by 2030. Final energy consumption is to be reduced using energy efficiency measures by at least 26.5% by 2030, from a 2008 baseline.
Document Title: Germany Updated Final National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP). 2021-2030

Family Name: Regulations Governing the Collection of Carbon Fees
Family Summary:
August 2024, Taiwan's Ministry of Environment (MOENV) announced three carbon fee related regulations that establish a carbon pricing system. The first regulation, entitled “Regulations Governing the Collection of Carbon Fees”, outlines how the carbon fees will be collected from entities.

Scope:

Entities subject to carbon fees: Power and gas supply industries, along with manufacturing industries emitting 25,000 metric tons or more of CO2e annually, will be subject to carbon fees.

Payment Timing:

Starting from the year after the fee rate takes effect, entities must pay carbon fees annually by the end of May. Payment is based on the total emissions of the preceding year, calculated using the announced rates. For instance, if the rates become effective on January 1, 2025, then payment for emissions during 2025 would be due by May 2026.

Transitional Adjustment Mechanism:

To ease the transition, a mechanism adjusts chargeable emissions, particularly for industries susceptible to carbon leakage, through an adjustment coefficient that increases over time. The emission adjustment coefficient value for the first period is 0.2, 0.4 for the second, and 0.6 for the third period.

Carbon credits:

Entities can utilize both domestic and carbon credits. Domestic credits can offset up to 10% of chargeable emissions. International credits require MOENV approval and can only be used by industries not considered high risk for carbon leakage.

Implementation Timeline:

Following a trial declaration without payment in 2025, payments based on 2025 emission levels will commence in 2026. The fee rate, to be determined by October 2024 and effective from January 1, 2025, will be reviewed annually.
Document Title: Regulations Governing the Collection of Carbon Fees

Family Name: CNPE Resolution 5 of August 26, 2024, on the National Energy Transition Policy (PNTE)
Family Summary:
This Resolution from the National Energy Policy Council (CNPE) establishes the National Energy Transition Policy (PNTE), the National Energy Transition Plan (Plante), the National Energy Transition Forum (Fonte), and makes other provisions. The Resolution establishes that the aim of the National Energy Transition Policy is to guide national efforts to transform the national energy matrix into a low-carbon economy, contributing to the achievement of net greenhouse gas emission neutrality in the country. The Policy consists of a mechanism to support the integration and coordination of government policies and actions at the federal level, in conjunction with sub-national entities, and for dialogue with civil society and the productive sector, to consolidate national efforts. It must observe the objectives of the national energy policy for the rational use of energy sources in harmony with the international policies and commitments made by the country concerning climate change. It must also consider the other objectives of public policies, including initiatives and strategies to enable the ecological transformation of the Brazilian economy, the increased density of production chains and adding value in the country, and mitigation and adaptation to climate change.

The CEFONTE Resolution from October 1st, 2025 defines the criteria for appointing members to the Plenary of the National Energy Transition Forum - Fonte.

The CEFONTE Resolution from January 13th, 2025 provides for the Regulation of the Public Selection Process for the selection of civil society representatives to make up the Plenary of the National Energy Transition Forum - Source Plenary, for the 2025/2026 biennium.
Document Title: Resolution CEFONTE 1 of January 13, 2025

Family Name: France Updated Final National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP). 2021-2030
Family Summary:
The National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) is a ten-year integrated document mandated by the European Union to each of its member states in order for the EU to meet its overall greenhouse gases emissions targets. The plan is based on two national energy and climate programming and governance documents. Firstly, the multi-year energy program, which sets the priorities for actions of the public authorities in the field of energy for the next 10 years, divided into two 5-year periods. It deals with all energies and all the pillars of energy policy: control of energy demand, promotion of renewable energies, guarantee of security of supply, control of energy costs, balanced development of networks, etc. Secondly, the national low-carbon strategy, which is France's roadmap for leading the climate change mitigation policy. It provides guidelines for implementing the transition to a low-carbon economy in all sectors of activity. It defines objectives for reducing greenhouse gas emissions at the scale of France in the short and medium term - carbon budgets - and aims to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. other Quantified goals include a 50% reduction in non-LULUCF GHG emissions by 2030, relative to 1990.
Document Title: France Updated Final National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP). 2021-2030

Family Name: Law on Forests (No. 011/24-1259/2-01)
Family Summary:
This Law regulates the cultivation, protection, preservation and improvement of forests, planning, methods and conditions of forest use, construction and maintenance of forest roads, forest monitoring, as well as other issues of importance for forests, forest land and forestry. It also applies to the protection, preservation and use of forest trees located outside forests.

This Law contains provisions on protecting the ecological functions of forests, which include the sequestration of carbon from the air, and on forest monitoring. Forest monitoring is carried out for the purpose of preservation, restoration and sustainable use of forest ecosystems and their services, to increase the resilience of forests and enable the protection of the multifunctionality of forests, with a special emphasis on adaptation and mitigation of climate change.
Document Title: Law on Forests (No. 011/24-1259/2-01)

Family Name: National Strategy for Agricultural Development (SENDA)
Family Summary: This document contains the National Strategy for Agricultural Development (SENDA), which is part of state policies aimed at increasing the productivity of agro-industrial chains, fishing, and aquaculture in a sustainable manner. SENDA thus contributes to the national goal of stimulating long-term economic growth, promoting social inclusion, and improving human well-being. SENDA also seeks to facilitate compliance with environmental commitments, such as the Paris Agreement (United Nations, 2015b) to combat climate change, the Sendai Framework (2015a) for disaster risk reduction, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022), and other multilateral environmental agreementsIn response to the Paris Agreement of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), Uruguay set the goal of reducing absolute emissions (in the Second Nationally Determined Contribution or NDC2) with specific targets for the agricultural sector - for instance stabilizing methane and nitrous oxide emissions to ensure they do not generate additional warming. Following a national and international diagnosis, the document outlines six strategic dimensions identified as key to organizing public policies for sector development, namely: 1) International integration; 2) Infrastructure and logistics; 3) Sustainability of agroecosystems; 4) Productive and social development; 5) Information technologies for agriculture; and 6) Institutional capacities.
Document Title: National Strategy for Agricultural Development (SENDA)

Family Name: Denmark Updated Final National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP). 2021-2030
Family Summary:
The National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) is a ten-year integrated document mandated by the European Union to each of its member states in order for the EU to meet its overall greenhouse gases emissions targets. Following feedback from an EU-wide assessment of draft NECP submissions, EU members are required to submit updated final NECPs for the period 2021-2030

The plan details key objectives and measures to achieve them: 1) decarbonisation : reduction of GHG emissions, transport green transition with a stop to sales of all new diesel and petrol cars as of 2030, ban on burning of straw residues on fields, public afforestation and a grant scheme for afforestation on private agricultural land and subsidy for conversion of arable land on organic soils to nature, etc; 2) renewable energy: three new offshore wind farms of at least 800 MW each, reduction of the electrical heating tax and of the electricity tax, support of geothermal energy, etc; 3) energy efficiency: to build a competitive subsidy scheme related to private enterprises, efficiency of existing buildings through renovation, etc; 4) energy security: stable energy supply thanks to laws on responsibilities regarding electricity supply, gas supply and emergency plans, prevention of risks in the energy system, increased international cooperation, interconnectivity concerning energy supply. Quantified targets include a 70% reduction of net GHG emissions by 2030, from a 1990 baseline.

Family Summary: This Decree establishes the Carbon Market Bureau in charge of setting up carbon credits and a national carbon registry along with institutional arrangements such as a supervisory council and technical secretariat.

Family Name: Canada’s 2030 Nature Strategy: Halting and Reversing Biodiversity Loss in Canada
Family Summary:
This national strategy establishes a shared vision and roadmap for halting and reversing biodiversity loss in Canada, laying the groundwork for transformative change. These six pillars ensure that the path to 2030 is inclusive, adaptable, and evidence-based:

  • Recognizing, upholding, and implementing the rights of Indigenous Peoples and advancing reconciliation, as Indigenous Peoples are the original caretakers of the lands, waters, and ice.
  • Ensuring a whole-of-government, whole-of-society approach to create policy coherence and draw on the strengths of every segment of society to build and deliver the solutions we need.
  • Supporting a resilient economy and improving efficiency and certainty, as our prosperity is inherently linked to a healthy environment.
  • Empowering on-the-ground action by reflecting regional differences, supporting communities, and adopting flexible community-based approaches.
  • Using the best available science and knowledge, incorporating new insights, sharing information, and giving equal weight to western science and Indigenous Knowledge.
  • Applying integrated, holistic approaches to ensure our actions are inclusive and transparent.

The strategy addresses all 23 of Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework targets - including Target 8 on minimising the impact of climate change and increasing the climate resilience of biodiversity - and builds on historic recent investments of more than $12B since 2018 in conservation, ecosystem restoration, species protection, and natural climate solutions. In relation to target 8, Canada will mitigate by reducing greenhouse gas emissions economy wide; implementing nature-based solutions; supporting ecosystem-based approaches; and advancing science and knowledge. Canada will adapt by implementing natural climate solutions; advancing science and knowledge; and developing tools and capacity. Canada will also consider cliamte change and biodiversity effects in decision-making, and foster positive impacts of climate action.

The federal government may also explore additional opportunities, including:

  • Advancing new and innovative solutions that address the nexus between climate change and biodiversity loss.
  • Developing an Ocean Climate Action Plan, which could include the use of climate information in decision making.
  • Enhancing our understanding of the impacts of climate change and ocean acidification on biodiversity in Canada's oceans, developing risk management and adaptation approaches, and gaining a better understanding of the carbon sequestration potential of our oceans.
  • Addressing knowledge gaps to support positive biodiversity conservation outcomes from boreal wildfire management response measures and associated forest management practices.
Document Title: Canada’s 2030 Nature Strategy: Halting and Reversing Biodiversity Loss in Canada

Family Name: Ordinance on State Aid for the Capture, Transport, and Storage of Biogenic CO2 (2024:626)
Family Summary:
The new regulation establishes a framework for state aid through reverse auctions, to incentivise CO2 capture and storage from biofuel combustion.

Through the reverse auction system, the Swedish Energy Agency will award funds to companies offering CO2 capture, transport, and storage at the lowest cost per tonne whilst also fulfilling certain other requirements. The aid is aimed at facilities located in Sweden, both during investment and operations phases. The Energy Agency can allocate 36 billion SEK (3 billion euro) between 2026 and 2046. In the first round, applications for aid under the Regulation can be submitted until 21 November 2024 and there has already been great interest in this. The Energy Agency aims to make a first allocation before the end of this year.

The scheme will run until 31 December 2028. By enabling capture and storage of significant amounts of biogenic CO2, the scheme will contribute to Sweden's efforts to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions by 85% by 2045 compared to the 1990 level. It will also help Sweden and the EU to meet the objective of achieving climate neutrality by 2050. The European Commission has approved this scheme, under EU State aid rules.
Document Title: Ordinance on State Aid for the Capture, Transport, and Storage of Biogenic CO2 (2024:626)

Family Name: Decree UP-106 On the Establishment of The Climate Council Under the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan
Family Summary: Decree UP-106 establishes a national climate council as the highest advisory body to the president on climate adaptation and mitigation, to better co-ordinate and unify national climate policy. The decree and formation of the council initiates the process of developing a national climate mitigation and adaptation strategy. Aside from strategic and legislative efforts, the decree also places emphasis on the expansion and integration of carbon trading systems nationally.

Family Name: Multiannual Sectoral Strategic Plan (PESEM) for the environmental sector 2024-2030 [Plan Estratégico Sectorial Multianual (PESEM) del sector ambiental 2024 – 2030]
Family Summary: Peru's Ministerial Resolution No. 105-2024-MINAM approves the Multi-Annual Strategic Sectoral Plan for the environmental sector 2024-2030, establishing the strategic framework for environmental governance across national, regional and local government entities within Peru's National Environmental Management System. The Plan articulates six strategic sectoral objectives that directly address climate change mitigation and adaptation whilst advancing the energy transition: reducing biodiversity degradation and ecosystem service loss; controlling environmental pollution across air, water and soil components; strengthening the transition to a circular economy with enhanced solid waste management; reducing climate risks and greenhouse gas emissions in alignment with Peru's Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement; improving decentralised environmental governance with territorial focus; and enhancing citizens' environmental behaviour. Of particular significance for climate action, Strategic Objective 4 explicitly addresses both adaptation and mitigation dimensions through measures to strengthen climate resilience of populations and ecosystems, implement sectoral GHG reduction strategies, and enhance climate risk monitoring and forecasting systems. The Plan operationalises Peru's commitments under the UNFCCC, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and broader sustainable development objectives, whilst responding to recommendations from the Environmental Performance Review and supporting Peru's OECD accession process.
Document Title: Multiannual Sectoral Strategic Plan (PESEM) for the environmental sector 2024-2030 [Plan Estratégico Sectorial Multianual (PESEM) del sector ambiental 2024 – 2030]

Family Name: Fifth Strategic Plan for Agricultural Transformation (PSTA5)
Family Summary: Rwanda's Fifth Strategic Plan for Agricultural Transformation (PSTA5) is a core planning document for short to medium-term agricultural policy and interventions. It underscores the importance of mitigating and adapting to climate change, and sets out a range of measures to develop the agri-food system while taking climate issues into account. Among three priority funding areas, 58.6% of the total strategic budget is allocated to modernisation and climate-resilience. These interventions include efficient irrigation and water storage systems, landscape-level interventions such as forest restoration and agroforestry, crop insurance mechanisms, and research to select and promote climate-resilient crop and animal varieties.
Document Title: Fifth Strategic Plan for Agricultural Transformation (PSTA5)

Family Name: National Environment Sector Plan (NESP) 2023-2027
Family Summary: Samoa's National Environment Sector Plan (NESP) for 2023-2027 aims to guide environmental conservation and sustainable development, noting climate change as a significant national and global threat to the environment. A priority of the plan is to enhance climate resilience and low-carbon technology across sectors, through land use and efficient natural resource consumption. It promotes forest restoration, improved hydrological and climate monitoring/warning systems, and general improvements in climate-resilience capacity across environmental education, governance and infrastructure project implementation.
Document Title: National Environment Sector Plan (NESP) 2023-2027

Family Name: Sustainable Finance Taxonomy
Family Summary:
This Taxonomy is a classification system that defines eligibility criteria and indicators to identify economic activities that contribute to the transition towards a sustainable, resilient and inclusive economy of the country. It is aligned with the 2021 Green Bond Principles, 2021 Social Bond Principles, and the Sustainable Bond Guide, published by the International Capital Market Association (ICMA).

This Taxonomy covers: nine sectors: Agriculture, livestock and forestry; water supply and treatment; manufacturing, waste management and emission capture; supply of electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning; construction; transport; information and communications technology; and financial and insurance activities.

This Taxonomy is the result of a joint effort led by the Panama Sustainable Finance Task Force (GTFS), the Superintendency of Banks of Panama (SBP), the Superintendency of the Securities Market of Panama (SMV), and the Superintendency of Insurance and Reinsurance of Panama (SSRP), in close collaboration with the Ministry of Environment (MiAmbiente) and the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF), and with the technical support of the United Nations Environment Programme Finance Initiative (UNEP FI), and the financial support of the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and the European Union, through its EUROCLIMA program.
Document Title: Sustainable Finance Taxonomy

Family Name: Decree PP-233 On Measures to Create a Climate-Resilient Agro-Ecosystem and Increase the Resilience of Agricultural Producers to the Risks Associated with Climate Change
Family Summary: Decree PP-233 implements a package of national and international funding for agricultural climate adaptation measures, setting priorities, responsibilities and subsequent action. Measures include ecosystem restoration, urban green space expansion, environmental early warning systems, anti-desertification afforestation, low-till agriculture implementation, climate action verification systems, on-site adaptation training seminars for land managers, and substantial media coverage of these issues and projects.
Document Title: Decree PP-233 On Measures to Create a Climate-Resilient Agro-Ecosystem and Increase the Resilience of Agricultural Producers to the Risks Associated with Climate Change

Family Name: Agricultural Agreement on a Green Denmark
Family Summary:
The Government and the parties in the Green Tripartite (Agriculture Food, the Danish Nature Conservation Association, the Danish Food Association NNF, Danish Metal, the Confederation of Danish Industry, etc.) have agreed on a long-term basis for the conversion and transformation of Denmark's land and food and agricultural production. The efforts in the agreement will reduce the sector's greenhouse gas emissions and contribute to meeting Denmark's 2030 climate goals, as well as ensuring better conditions for nature, biodiversity, the aquatic environment and drinking water. This will include a historic land conversion and a tax on emissions from livestock. At the same time, the agreement sets the direction for a more sustainable, high-tech and land-efficient agriculture with competitiveness and good jobs throughout the country.

With the agreement, the parties agree that a CO2e tax on emissions from livestock will be introduced. A tax of DKK 300 per ton CO2e will be introduced in 2030, increasing to DKK 750 per ton CO2e in 2035 with a base deduction of 60 percent. The effective tax will therefore amount to DKK 120 per ton CO2e in 2030, increasing to DKK 300 per ton CO2e in 2035. tons of CO2e in 2035. In addition, a good 30 billion kroner will be allocated for the removal of a total of approximately 140,000 ha of carbon-rich lowland soils including marginal areas and the establishment of 250,000 ha of forest. In addition, a subsidy scheme of a total of just over 10 billion kroner will be established towards 2045 for the storage of biochar produced by pyrolysis.

Overall, the efforts in the agreement are estimated to reduce Danish emissions by 1.8 million tons of CO2e in 2030. The agreement thus closes the gap in relation to the 2030 climate target.
Document Title: Agricultural Agreement on a Green Denmark

Family Name: Agreement on a Green Denmark (2024)
Family Summary:
In the summer of 2024, the parties behind the Green Tripartite entered into the historic Agreement on a Green Denmark, which is to ensure more nature, cleaner water and a sustainable transformation of agriculture. Later that year, the SVM government made the political agreement  Implementation of a Green Denmark  with the SF, Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People's Party and the Radical Left, which ensures broad support for the implementation of the tripartite agreement. The agreements are among the most ambitious green agreements in Danish history, and they are agreements that are not only about environmental improvements, but also about ensuring that Denmark can continue to be a pioneer in the green transition.

The agreements have been concluded by the government together with a number of political parties and organizations in the Green Tripartite, including:

  • The government, as well as the SF, the Danish Social Democratic Party, the Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People's Party
  • The National Association of Municipalities (KL)
  • Agriculture Food
  • Danish Nature Conservation Society
  • The Norwegian Food Federation (NNF)
  • Danish Metal
  • Danish Industry

The broad support must ensure that the agreement takes into account nature, the climate and the industries affected by the changes.

The agreements involve a comprehensive restructuring of Denmark's land area and a number of initiatives to protect the environment and reduce climate impact. The most important elements are:

  • 250,000 hectares of new forest, equivalent to the areas of Lolland, Falster and Bornholm combined.
  • Conversion of 140,000 hectares of low-lying agricultural land that emits a lot of CO 2 when cultivated. Some of this land will be converted to nature instead.
  • More biodiversity, including through the creation of 21 new national nature parks, one urban national nature park and improvement of the marine environment in the Little Belt and Øresund.
  • Strengthened efforts for the aquatic environment to reduce oxygen depletion in Danish fjords and coastal areas.
  • CO2 tax on livestock production: Denmark will be the first country in the world to introduce this type of tax. 
  • Forward-looking, competitive and sustainable Danish food production with increased focus on biosolutions, climate technologies and plant-based foods.
  • 43 billion kroner to Danmarks Grønne Arealfond, which will finance green initiatives.
  • 23 local tripartite partnerships, where municipalities, the state and representatives from Agriculture Food and the Danish Nature Conservation Association collaborate to convert agricultural areas to nature.
Document Title: Agreement on the Implementation of a Green Denmark (2024)

Family Name: National Family Farming Plan 2024-2028
Family Summary:
The National Family Farming Plan of Uruguay is adopted within the framework of the United Nations’ Decade of Family Farming (2019-2028) and FAO’s and FIDA’s Worldwide Action Plan. This document will guide policies from 2024 to 2028, emphasizing the crucial role that family farming plays in various value chains across the country. After providing the background (legal and institutional framework for family farming) and assessing the current situation and its challenges, the plan outlines strategies for the 2024-2028 period, including implementation strategies such as monitoring, governance, and evaluation.

The National Family Farming Plan (PNAF) is organized around the following key pillars: 1) Legal and institutional framework; 2) Youth; 3) Gender; 4) Organizations; 5) Socioeconomic inclusion and well-being; 6) Sustainability, environment, and climate change; 7) Territory and multidimensionality.

Pillar 6, focusing on Sustainability, Environment, and Climate Change, includes specific actions such as integrating family farming into medium and long-term water sector strategies and addressing its needs; developing risk management tools for family farming; institutionalizing the climate change and family farming perspective in the General Directorate of Rural Development (DGDR); creating methodological guides for systematically including family farming in climate change plans and programs; raising awareness in the family farming sector about biodiversity and related regulations; and coordinating the implementation of both the PNAF and the National Agroecology Plan.
Document Title: National Family Farming Plan 2024-2028

Family Name: Green Taxonomy
Family Summary:
The Green Taxonomy of the Dominican Republic (TVRD) is a classification system of economic and asset activities that contribute substantially to the achievement of environmental and/or social objectives, aligning with the commitments, strategies and policies outlined by the country. The TVRD acts as a reference framework that seeks to promote initiatives that support both sustainable development and the transition to a low-carbon economy.

The beginning of taxonomy work began in 2020 with the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the International Financial Corporation (IFC) of the World Bank group and the Superintendence of the Securities Market where the action plan was worked to address the taxonomy development project.

The TVRD covers economic ativities that contribute to the environmental objectives of climate change mitigation and adaptation, the sustainable use and protection of water and coastal-marine resources and economic sectors of greater relevance: water and water resources, waste management and emission capture, transport, energy, construction and industry.
Document Title: Green Taxonomy

Family Name: Action Plan for Low-Carbon Transformation and Construction of Coal Power Plants (2024-2027)
Family Summary:
This action plan has been formulated to coordinate the low-carbon transformation of existing coal-fired power units and the low-carbon construction of new coal-fired power units, improve the clean and efficient use of coal, accelerate the construction of a new clean, low-carbon, safe and efficient energy system, and contribute to the achievement of carbon peak and carbon neutrality goals.

By 2025, all of the first batch of low-carbon coal-fired power transformation and construction projects will have commenced, and a number of low-carbon coal-fired power generation technologies will have been converted and applied. The carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour of these projects will be approximately 20% lower than the average carbon emissions of similar coal-fired power units in 2023, significantly lower than the carbon emissions of currently operating advanced coal-fired power units, and thus explore useful experience for the clean and low-carbon transformation of coal-fired power. By 2027, the technology routes for low-carbon coal-fired power generation will be further expanded, and construction and operation costs will be significantly reduced. The carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour of related projects will be reduced by about 50% compared with the average carbon emissions level of similar coal-fired power units in 2023, and close to the carbon emissions level of natural gas power generation units, forming a strong leading and driving role in the clean and low-carbon transformation of coal-fired power. Transformation methods include biomass co-firing, green ammonia co-firing and carbon capture, utilisation and storage.
Document Title: Action Plan for Low-Carbon Transformation and Construction of Coal Power Plants (2024-2027)

Family Name: Agricultural Agreement 2024 (Prop. 105 S (2023-2024))
Family Summary:
This Agreement was entered into between the state, the Norwegian Farmers' Association and the Norwegian Farmers' and Small Farmers' Association on 16 May 2024, and subsequently approved by Parliament. One of the policy areas is climate, nature and the environment. It was agreed that the agricultural agreement will be turned in a more climate- and environmentally-friendly direction, and will contribute to maintaining the cultural landscape and to reducing the environmental impact from agriculture, including emissions to air and water.

Actions include:

  • Follow-up of the climate agreement between the state and agricultural organizations by strengthening the knowledge base on climate measures, measures that contribute to reduced emissions, increased absorption and better climate adaptation, including increased support for drainage, biogas and other fertilizer measures and hydrotechnical facilities.
  • Follow-up of the Comprehensive Action Plan for the Oslo Fjord with strengthening of grant funds to stimulate the implementation of runoff reduction measures.
  • Follow-up of the government's focus on nature through grazing schemes, pasture subsidies and other schemes that contribute to maintaining and improving the values ​​of the agricultural cultural landscape.
  • A significant investment in fruit and vegetables.
Document Title: Agricultural Agreement 2024 (Prop. 105 S (2023-2024))

Family Name: Climate Change Mitigation Strategy and Action Plan 2024-2030
Family Summary:
This document aims to present a roadmap on climate response covering the period until 2030 and includes the relevant strategies and action plans in this regard. Built on a scientific basis, it offers a comprehensive approach by bringing together institutional policies, expert views, and GHG reduction needs. It includes 49 strategies and 260 actions covering GHG reduction policies in energy, industry, buildings, transport, waste, agriculture, and land use, land use change and forestry (LULUCF) sectors as well as in areas of carbon pricing mechanisms and just transition.

The key sectoral strategies in the Action Plan, which comprises 49 strategies and 260 actions for 7 main mitigation sectors and 2 cross-cutting thematic areas, include:

● Promoting energy efficiency across all sectors,

● Maximising the use of renewable energy,

● Reducing product-based carbon footprint and carbon intensity in industry,

● Promoting sustainability reporting,

● Promoting circular economy and resource efficiency across the manufacturing industry,

● Promoting Nearly Zero Energy buildings,

● Promoting the use of district heating and cooling systems,

● Developing electrification systems in the transport sector,

● Developing integrated transport systems,

● Ensuring transition to zero- or low-emission transport systems,

● Protecting and increasing sink areas for effective climate response,

● Ensuring transition of forestry and agricultural enterprises to circular bioeconomy with high added value,

● Extending eco-friendly agricultural practices,

● Ensuring rational fertiliser use,

● Reducing methane emissions originating from livestock,

● Preventing and reducing waste generation,

● Increasing use of waste as raw material/resource in production,

● Establishing an emissions trading system in Türkiye,

● Conducting infrastructure studies on other carbon pricing mechanisms,

● Developing and promoting clean technologies,

● Achieving digitalization in all sectors,

● Developing incentive and support mechanisms for GHG reduction,

● Developing sustainable investment instruments,

● Planning for transition to a low-carbon economy with the principle of just transition,

● Building capacity for just transition and employment transformation, and

● Integrating Türkiye’s net zero emission target into the education system.
Document Title: Climate Change Mitigation Strategy and Action Plan 2024-2030

Family Name: National Ecological Transition Strategy
Family Summary: Tunisia's National Ecological Transition Strategy aims to guide sustainable economic development across a wide range of sectors while preserving and restoring natural capital. The strategy underscores the need to adapt to climate change and reduce the carbon intensity of the economy. Among other measures, it promotes: development of climate-specific policies and the formation of government entities to oversee their implementation; creation of a national climate early warning system; intensification of reforestation efforts; substantial waste reductions across the economy; enhanced flood protection; sustainable urban mobility.
Document Title: National Ecological Transition Strategy

Family Name: Climate Change (Carbon Markets) Regulations 2024
Family Summary: Establishes a formal legal framework for carbon markets in Kenya under the Climate Change Act, organising the certification, verification, and operation of carbon credit programmes, in addition to defining core principles such as additionality, permanence, and double counting. It aims to integrate sustainable development benefits, and enhance the transparency and market oversight of carbon credit activities, while taking environmental and social safeguards into account to support Kenya in meeting its climate commitments. It institutionalises a Designated National Authority responsible for overseeing transactions, compliance, and preventing double counting.
Document Title: Climate Change (Carbon Markets) Regulations 2024

Family Name: Circular of May 14, 2024, no. 22 - Updated Operational Guide for compliance with the principle of not causing significant harm to the environment (DNSH)
Family Summary: Under Article 18 of EU Regulation 241/2021, every reform and investment within a National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP) must strictly adhere to the "Do No Significant Harm" (DNSH) principle. To support government bodies and project leads in navigating these technical requirements, the State General Accounting Office (Ragioneria Generale dello Stato) issued Circular No. 22 of May 14, 2024, which introduces the third edition of the DNSH Operational Guide. The guide brings climate and energy-related requirements and checklists to be fulfilled. Essentially, Circular 22/2024 acts as the definitive technical manual for ensuring that Italy’s green transition investments are legally compliant and eligible for continued EU funding.

Collection Name: Law 7/2021 on climate change and energy transition [Spain]
Collection Summary:
Enacted in 2021, this law establishes Spain's legal framework for achieving climate neutrality by 2050, aligning with the Paris Agreement and Sustainable Development Goals. It mandates a 23% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 (compared to 1990 levels), alongside ambitious renewable energy targets, including 42% of final energy consumption from renewables and 74% renewable electricity generation by 2030. Energy efficiency measures aim for a 39.5% reduction in primary energy consumption within the same timeframe. The law also prohibits new hydrocarbon and radioactive mineral exploitation, requires emission-free transport systems in cities with populations exceeding 50,000, and emphasises sustainable urban mobility.

The legislation includes a national Just Transition Strategy to ensure equitable economic opportunities, particularly for vulnerable regions, while fostering adaptation and resilience to climate risks across critical sectors such as water, biodiversity, and health. It creates governance mechanisms like the Expert Committee on Climate Change and Energy Transition to monitor progress and updates to Spain's Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan (PNIEC). Projecting investments exceeding €200 billion by 2030, the law is expected to enhance Spain’s GDP by €16.5–25.7 billion annually and generate 250,000–350,000 new jobs. The focus on education, innovation, and public awareness underscores its commitment to a holistic and inclusive transition.

This collection represent a body of policies, strategies, and plans enacted under this law.
Family Name: State Plan for Scientific, Technical, and Innovation Research 2024-2027 (PEICTI)
Family Summary: The State Plan for Scientific, Technical, and Innovation Research 2024-2027 (PEICTI) is a strategic framework developed under Spain’s Law on Science, Technology, and Innovation (Law 14/2011). It serves as the multi-annual instrument for planning and coordinating state-led policies in research, development, and innovation (RDI) within the framework of the Spanish Strategy for Science, Technology, and Innovation 2021-2027 (EECTI). The PEICTI outlines specific objectives derived from the EECTI and includes detailed programmes and actions to be implemented by various government departments and affiliated organisations, including public research institutions. The plan requires strong inter-ministerial collaboration and is classified as a strategic subsidies plan under Spain’s General Subsidies Law.Aligned with the European Green Transition policies, the PEICTI integrates eco-responsibility principles, such as the Do No Significant Harm (DNSH) approach and carbon-neutral infrastructure development. It supports circularity in research projects and aims to enhance public engagement on ecological and climate issues. The plan considered and plays a role in advancing Spain’s National Energy and Climate Plan (PNIEC) 2023-2030, contributing to research and innovation for sustainable development.
Document Title: State Plan for Scientific, Technical, and Innovation Research 2021-2023 (PEICTI)

Family Summary:
This plan came as the fourth phase of the national development plans starting in 2010, which represents a state of integration and interconnectedness to achieve Iraq’s vision 2030 in sustainable development, with its targets and programs that overlap and align with the state’s development trends and priorities at this stage, starting with the governance of effective development institutions, through economic reform programs and reforming the business environment for the private sector, digital transformations and reducing development gaps, improving human capital and dealing with the repercussions of climate change.

  • Diversifying the productive structure of the national economy;
  • Improving the performance efficiency of the infrastructure and community services sector.
  • Implementing climate change mitigation and adaptation policies and strengthening responsive partnerships.
  • Increasing the efficiency of fiscal and monetary policy tools to meet the requirements of economic reform.

Family Name: Norway’s integrated ocean management plans (Meld. St. 21 2023-2024)
Family Summary:
The purpose of the management plans is to provide a framework for value creation through the sustainable use of marine natural resources and ecosystem services and at the same time maintain ecosystem structure, functioning, productivity and diversity. The management plans are thus a tool both for facilitating value creation and food security, and for maintaining the high environmental value of Norway’s seas and oceans.

The plans include the climate and environmental considerations as a basis for marine spatial management; adaptation to climate change and a warmer ocean; and strengthening the knowledge base on oceans and climate change. Norway is considering carbon capture and storage under the seabed, aided by the presence of geological formations suitable for carbon dioxide storage, as an important mitigation measure in climate policy.
Document Title: Norway’s integrated ocean management plans (Meld. St. 21 2023-2024)

Family Name: Seychelles National Development Strategy 2024-2028
Family Summary: The Seychelles National Development Strategy 2024-2028 aims to provide an overarching framework to guide sustainable socioeconomic development, and notes climate change mitigation and adaptation as a major risk and practical challenge for the country. The strategy identifies agriculture, digital economy, fisheries and blue economy more generally as key sectors for growth. As balanced outcomes across the economy it prioritises: public service modernisation; general economic transformation; improved public health; law and order; a modernised and forward-looking education system; environmental sustainability and climate change resilience. On climate change the strategy seeks to diversify the export economy to reduce vulnerability to fisheries supply shocks, build capacity for coastal and marine ecosystem/infrastructure protection, and increase the renewables share of energy to 25% by 2030, also increasing energy efficiency to reduce the carbon intensity of the economy.

Family Summary:
This regulation sets out the rules for operations related to Climate Action and Sustainability, funded by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) and the Cohesion Fund (CF), for the programming period 2021-2027. The regulation covers specific objectives related to the Portugal 2030 programs, including:

Energy efficiency and decarbonization in regional and local public administration.
Promotion of self-consumption and renewable energy communities.
Energy storage, better management, and increased digitalization of energy grids.
Climate change adaptation, risk management, and water resource management.
Coastal protection and defence.
Urban water cycle management.
Urban waste management.
Conservation of nature, biodiversity, and natural heritage.
Environmental liabilities, such as abandoned mining sites.
Promoting multimodal sustainable urban mobility as part of the transition to a zero-carbon economy.

Article 11 defines the conditions for funding allocation towards climate goals, prioritising sustainable projects that help to meet climate targets on circular economy, public infrastructure and housing renovation, water supply and contaminated land that becomes a carbon sink.

Family Name: OGA Plan on Emissions Reduction
Family Summary: The Plan is a regulatory instrument issued under the NSTA's overarching OGA Strategy, translating that Central Obligation into concrete, binding requirements, including cutting emissions from flaring, venting, and power generation, and supporting CCUS to help the UK meet net zero by 2050. Rather than setting a single interim target or target year, the Plan lays out binding principles and requirements operators must follow, organised under four headings: investment and efficiency, electrification and low-carbon power, flaring and venting, and inventory. Crucially, emissions offsetting does not count toward meeting these obligations, only actual reductions do.

Family Name: The Green Industrial Initiative (Roadmap 2.0)
Family Summary: This roadmap aims to help Norway achieve its target of cutting climate emissions by 50% by 2030. The roadmap will also help boost Norwegian exports. This plan focuses on access to renewable energy, infrastructure, technology, and capital. The plan highlights nine priority sectors for green initiatives, including: offshore wind production, low-emission hydrogen production and distribution, CCSU, battery value chain development, energy-efficient process industry, solar industry, forestry, manufacturing, and maritime activities. The original initiative was launched by the Norwegian Government in 2022, and this updated "Roadmap 2.0" was launched in 2024.
