Collection Name: The Mother Earth Law and Integral Development to Live Well, Framework Law No 300
Collection Summary:
The Mother Earth Law is a piece of legislation that epitomises Bolivia's dedication to sustainable development, respecting the balance between human life and the natural environment, and prioritising the rights and knowledge of the country's majority indigenous population. The expressed objective of the law is to 'establish the vision and fundamentals of integral development in harmony and balance with Mother Earth to Live Well, guaranteeing the continued capacity of Mother Earth to regenerate natural systems, recuperating and strengthening local and ancestral practices, within the framework of rights, obligations and responsibilities'.
 
 In relation to climate change the law has many provisions that outline the state's vision, citizens' rights, and responsibilities. It embraces the concept of 'climate justice', defined by the ability of all Bolivian citizens to 'Live Well', especially those who are most vulnerable to climate change. It reinforces the point that some states have more of a global responsibility to respond to climate change.
 
 To encourage sustainable development of natural resources, it states that climate change trajectories should be accounted for when planning and zoning responsible land use.
 
 The law focuses on reducing the risks posed by climate change through six lines of actions:
The permanent incorporation of prevention of and managed response to natural disasters into the System of Integral Planning
Risk management for the agricultural sector to prevent diminished crop yields and food insecurity
The adoption of risk management of disasters as well as adaption to climate change across state development projects; development of informational networks to issue early warnings in times of natural crisis as well as to assist the agricultural industry and indigenous communities plan according to climate conditions
Strengthening territorial management processes of sub-national governments through the incorporation of risk management and adaption to climate change perspectives
Articulation between public and private scientific research sectors to share knowledge and co-ordinate research regarding vulnerabilities related to climate change
 
 The Law defines 'Living Well' in relation to climate change and lays out the state's legal obligations. The state will develop policies, strategies and legal techniques to mitigate the effects of climate change and adapt to them through strengthening institutional capacities for the monitoring of climate with the purpose of long-term planning. The state will also encourage the recuperation of traditional indigenous practices that were historically sustainable and allowed for the natural regeneration of resources.
 
 The law also establishes the Plurinational Authority of Mother Earth, within the Ministry of Environment and Water, as the state entity responsible for much of the development, overseeing and co-ordination of projects, programmes and research as it relates to climate change and the objectives of the Plurinational Plan for Climate Change. It also co-ordinates scientific monitoring of GHG emissions. The entity will operate within the framework of 'climate justice,' following the principles of Bolivia's climate change politics.
 
 The Authority will operate through three mechanisms: (1) Joint Mechanism of Mitigation and Adaptation for the Integral and Sustainable Management of Mother Earth's Forests; (2) Mitigation Mechanism to 'Living Well'; and (3) Adaptation Mechanism to 'Living Well'.
 
 The Authority is also responsible for the management of the Plurinational Fund of Mother Earth. The Fund will be financed with multilateral and bilateral aid, public money from the national government allocated to mitigation or adaptation, funds from private donors, national or international loans, and funds at the disposal of the executive branch.
Family Name: Bolivian Plurinational Policy on Climate Change (PPCC), promoting integrated development in harmony with Mother Earth
Family Summary:
The Plurinational Policy on Climate Change (PPCC), updated in 2023 by Bolivia's Plurinational Authority of Mother Earth, provides a comprehensive framework for managing the climate crisis. Rooted in Law 300 (Law of Mother Earth and Integral Development for Living Well), the policy integrates ancestral knowledge and innovative strategies to address the dual challenges of mitigation and adaptation, aiming to protect the rights of Mother Earth while fostering sustainable development under the paradigm of Living Well (Vivir Bien).
The Bolivian Plurinational Policy adopts an interdisciplinary approach with four strategic pillars: (1) an integrated focus on forest and Mother Earth management; (2) climate mitigation, emphasising the energy, industrial, and service sectors; (3) climate adaptation and resilience in vulnerable regions; and (4) cross-cutting actions ensuring transparency, gender equity, and intergenerational justice.
These efforts aim to be aligned with Bolivia's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement, which target emission reductions and the preservation of ecosystems, including reducing deforestation by 80% and achieving universal access to resilient water systems by 2030. Operationally, the PPCC leverages mechanisms like the Joint Mitigation and Adaptation Mechanism and sectoral contributions to enhance forest conservation, renewable energy transitions, and sustainable agriculture. It underscores non-market approaches to climate finance, rejecting commodification of environmental functions. Guided by principles of climate justice, the PPCC addresses structural drivers of the climate crisis, advocating for collective global responsibility and the repayment of historical climate debts by developed nations.
Document Title: Bolivian Plurinational Policy on Climate Change (PPCC), promoting integrated development in harmony with Mother Earth

Family Name: Biomass Strategy
Family Summary: The Biomass Strategy 2023 sets out the UK Government’s approach to using sustainable biomass as part of the transition to net zero, recognising biomass as a limited resource that should be prioritised where it offers the greatest emissions-reduction potential and where alternatives are limited. The strategy places strong emphasis on strengthening sustainability criteria to ensure biomass delivers genuine greenhouse gas savings, while assessing future domestic and imported biomass availability. It identifies harder-to-decarbonise sectors and, in the longer term, Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage (BECCS) as priority uses, with BECCS expected to provide negative emissions that help balance residual emissions from sectors that are difficult to fully decarbonise. It also considers biomass’s role in renewable power, biomethane, heat, low-carbon transport fuels, industrial decarbonisation and low-carbon hydrogen, while highlighting the need to manage competing demands for sustainable biomass and protect wider environmental objectives.
Document Title: Biomass Strategy

Family Name: FRA BOD Decree 163/2023: Promulgating the Standards of Registering Verification and validation Bodies for Carbon Emission Reduction Projects With FRA.
Family Summary:
Within the context of Decree No. 4664/2022 that creates a voluntary market for trading carbon credits, Decree 163/2023 focuses on the registration process for Validation and Verification Bodies (VVBs) with the Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA) in Egypt.

Article 1 announces the creation of a registry within the FRA specifically for approving VVBs for carbon emission reduction projects. This registry serves as a centralised database containing detailed information on each approved VVB. Only VVBs listed in this registry are authorised to conduct verification and validation for carbon emission reduction projects intended for trading in Egypt.

Eligibility Criteria for Egyptian VVBs

1. Legal Entity: The applying entity must be a legally registered corporate entity in Egypt.

2. ISO Certifications: The entity must hold certifications demonstrating adherence to international standards for validating and verifying environmental information and greenhouse gas statements. The required certifications include ISO 14065:2020, ISO/IEC 17029:2019, and ISO 14064-3:2019.

3. Professional Competence: The VVB must demonstrate its professional capability to perform the required verification and validation tasks.

4. CEO Interview: The CEO or a designated representative must successfully complete an interview conducted by the FRA. This ensures that the leadership of the VVB understands the requirements and expectations of the FRA.

5. Clean Criminal Record: The management team and personnel involved in verification and validation must not have been convicted of felonies or misdemeanors related to crimes against honor or trust within the past three years, unless their rights have been fully restored. This provision aims to maintain the integrity and trustworthiness of the VVBs.

Eligibility Critieria for International VVBs

- The entity must be recognized by established international climate organizations, such as being a Designated Operational Entity (DOE) under the UNFCCC, recognized under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, or listed in international voluntary carbon registries like the Gold Standard, VCS, or GCC.

- The VVB must submit documentation showcasing its expertise and experience in verification and validation, including at least three projects registered in recognized international voluntary carbon registries.

- The VVB must include at least one Egyptian expert within its verification and validation team.

Additional Provisions

- Trading guidelines: International entities trading carbon emission reduction certificates within Egypt must notify the FRA of their accredited VVBs.

- Application Procedure: VVBs must submit applications using the FRA's designated form, along with documentation proving compliance with decree criteria. The FRA reviews complete submissions within 30 days.

-Registration Maintenance: VVBs must adhere to registration terms, comply with their commitments, and renew annually.

- Registration fees: For Egyptian VVBs (EGP 10,000 initial, EGP 2,000 renewal); international VVBs (USD 500 initial, USD 100 renewal).
Document Title: FRA BOD Decree 163/2023: Promulgating the Standards of Registering Verification and validation Bodies for Carbon Emission Reduction Projects With FRA.

Family Name: National Biodiversity Strategy 2030
Family Summary:
In line with the objectives of the European Biodiversity Strategy to 2030 and the Ecological Transition Plan, it outlines a vision for the future and development centered on the need to reverse the current trend of biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse.On August 3, 2023, Ministerial Decree No. 252 was signed, adopting the new National Biodiversity Strategy to 2030 and establishing its governing bodies.There are 18 actions distributed across the eight areas of intervention, for instance:

  • Legally protect at least 30% of the land area and 30% of the marine area through an integrated system of protected areas, the Natura 2000 network, and other legally protected areas.
  • Ensure that at least one-third of legally protected terrestrial and marine areas, including all primary and old-growth forests, are strictly protected.
  • Ensure the ecological and functional connectivity of protected areas at the local, national, and supranational levels.
  • Ensure adequate funding for protection
  • Ensure that for at least 30% of the species and habitats protected under the Birds and Habitats Directives whose conservation status is currently unsatisfactory, it becomes satisfactory by 2030 or shows a clear positive trend.
  • Ensure that all ecosystems do not deteriorate and that large areas of degraded ecosystems are restored, particularly those most suitable for capturing and storing carbon as well as for preventing and reducing the impact of natural disasters.
  • Achieve land degradation neutrality and zero net land-use change, and make significant progress in the remediation and restoration of degraded and contaminated land.
Document Title: Ministerial Decree 252/2023

Family Name: National Strategy for the Use of Carbon Markets (ENUMeC)
Family Summary:
The National Strategy for the Use of Carbon Markets (ENUMeC) in the Argentine Republic is a framework that facilitates the development of carbon markets with the objective of reducing emissions and promoting sustainable development. These markets allow companies and governments to buy and sell emission rights, thus incentivizing emissions reduction and environmental compensation. The ENUMeC deepens the national position regarding the use of carbon markets and creates a common framework for their implementation in the national territory. Among the axes of the strategy are:

- Strengthen national and subnational access to climate financing.

- Participate in carbon markets regulated in the Paris Agreement and other national and international compliance markets.

- Accompany the participation of the private sector in voluntary markets.

- Generate non-commercial approaches and support subnational governments in the implementation of market schemes to fulfill their climate change response plans.
Document Title: National Strategy for the Use of Carbon Markets (ENUMeC)

Family Name: Resolution 95/2023 on Sustainable Land Management
Family Summary: This Resolution (pages 2283 to 2287 of the Gazette) establishes the provision for granting recognition to Sustainable Land Management, which is a working strategy contributing to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals, specifically those related to food security, sustainable water management, biodiversity and terrestrial ecosystems and combating climate change, including neutrality in land degradation. It contains provisions on the requirements for obtaining recognition of sustainable land management; the application process; the group of expert evaluators; the approval and granting process; and the control of recognition and revocation.
Document Title: Resolution 95/2023 on Sustainable Land Management

Family Name: The National Strategy regarding the prevention and combating of desertification and land degradation 2021-2030
Family Summary:
Given the negative consequences of desertification and land degradation, this strategy aims to prevent and mitigate these processes by applying integrated measures aimed at long-term resource management. These measures will contribute to achieving land degradation and desertification neutrality by meeting the objectives and targets set by the 2030 Agenda to which Romania has committed itself to implement at national level. 

It includes the target to by 2030, combat desertification, land restoration and degraded land and soils, including land affected by desertification, drought and floods; and strive to achieve a land degradation neutral world, but also other interlinked objectives. 

The implementation period of the National Strategy on Preventing and Combating Desertification and Land Degradation is 2021-2030.

Specific objectives that will underpin the achievement of the overall objective to be met through the Strategy are the following:

1. Centralisation and evaluation of the data obtained from studies on the phenomenon of desertification in Romania carried out to date.

2. Analysis of the progress made at national level in the field of combatingdesertification

3. Identification and assessment of the projected environmental effects of the Strategy based on two scenarios: in the absence of the Strategy and by meeting the recommendations.

4. Establishment of measures to prevent, reduce, compensate and monitor effects of desertification on the environment according to the three scenarios.

5. Provide technical assistance/advice to the Ministry of Environment, Water and Forests on desertification until the completion of the contracted works.

6. Informing the public about desertification by organising debates and public consultations on the National Strategy on Prevention and Control of Desertification.

7. Drawing up the environmental report in accordance with the legal requirements in force and its endorsement by the competent authorities.

8. Preparation of the appropriate assessment study in accordance with the legal requirements in force. in force and its endorsement by the competent authorities.

9. Elaboration of the National Strategy on Prevention and Combating Desertification and Land Degradation and its endorsement by the competent authorities.
Document Title: The National Strategy regarding the prevention and combating of desertification and land degradation 2021-2030

Family Name: Carbon Capture Storage and Use (CCUS) Strategy
Family Summary:
In June 2023, the French government released a draft CCUS strategy for consultation with industry.


In its strategy, the government outlines carbon capture targets for France that include:

  • 4 to 8.5 million tons of CO2 captured a year by 2030 
  • 15 to 20 million tons of CO2 captured a year by 2050 
  • an extra 10 million tons of CO2 captured a year in non-industrial sectors around 2050.


The strategy is built on the principle that CCUS should not be used to maintain a “business as usual” approach but to be used to manage residual emissions in the absence of other solutions for decarbonisation or as a transition solution.


Actions in the draft strategy include:

  • carrying out an assessment of the potential of storage by the end of 2023 or beginning of 2024 
  • launching a call for tenders for seismic surveys and test injections of CO2 in pilot sites, with initial tests starting in 2024-2025
  • launching a support scheme via contracts for difference (CCFD) to support industry decarbonisation projects, in particular in the service of carbon capture and sequestration.
Document Title: Draft Carbon Capture, Storage and Use (CCUS) Strategy

Family Name: Environmental Land Management (ELM) update (2023)
Family Summary: The Environmental Land Management (ELM) update sets out the UK Government’s approach to reforming agricultural support in England by phasing out subsidies based primarily on land ownership and replacing them with payments for environmental, climate and sustainable farming outcomes. It establishes three complementary schemes: the Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI) for universal, straightforward sustainable farming practices; Countryside Stewardship (CS), including CS Plus, for more targeted habitat, landscape and environmental actions; and Landscape Recovery for bespoke, long-term, large-scale projects. The schemes are intended to support food production while delivering benefits including improved soil and water quality, biodiversity recovery, flood and drought resilience, woodland creation, carbon reduction and carbon storage. The update also outlines the expansion and refinement of SFI and CS, including new standards, more flexible agreements, quarterly payments and improved access for tenants, alongside competitive funding for Landscape Recovery projects. Overall, the document represents a key policy framework for England’s agricultural transition, with government aiming to increase participation in environmental land-management schemes while redirecting the farming budget towards environmental outcomes alongside food production.
Document Title: Environmental Land Management (ELM) update (2023)

Family Name: Ministerial Agreement No. MAATE-2021-047: Technical Standard for the Ecuador Carbon Zero Program with Organisational Scope
Family Summary: This Ministerial Agreement establishes the guidelines and technical criteria for implementing the Ecuador Carbon Zero Program (PECC) at an organisational level, aligning with Ecuador’s constitutional provisions on environmental sustainability, the living well (buen-vivir or sumak kawsay) and the rights of nature. It enables organisations (public, private, national, or international) to voluntarily measure, reduce, and neutralise their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from operational activities. The program applies a tiered certification system to encourage participants to advance from carbon footprint quantification (Level 1) to emission reduction (Level 2) and ultimately achieve carbon neutrality (Level 3).Proponents must develop an inventory of their organisational GHG emissions, covering direct (Scope 1), indirect (Scope 2), and selected value-chain emissions (Scope 3) for neutrality certification. The program follows international standards, such as the ISO 14064 series and the GHG Protocol, ensuring consistent methodologies for emission accounting and verification. Participants are required to set reduction targets, implement mitigation projects (e.g. renewable energy adoption, energy efficiency, and waste management) and engage in ongoing monitoring and reporting. Remaining emissions can be offset through nationally regulated compensation schemes.
Document Title: Ministerial Agreement No. MAATE-2021-047: Technical Standard for the Ecuador Carbon Zero Program with Organisational Scope

Family Name: Ministerial Agreement No. MAATE-2023-053. Technical standard for Ecuador's Greenhouse Gas Emissions Compensation Scheme
Family Summary: Rooted on constitutional provisions on sustainability, living well philosophy (Buen Vivir - Sumak Kawsay), this agreement establishes the regulatory framework for Ecuador’s National Greenhouse Gas Emissions Compensation Scheme, designed to facilitate voluntary initiatives that reduce or remove GHG emissions through mitigation projects. It applies to public, private, community, or mixed-sector initiatives developed within Ecuador, allowing national and international stakeholders to offset their carbon footprints by supporting certified projects. The scheme supports the broader goals of Ecuador's climate commitments, including the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement.The compensation scheme includes mechanisms for creating and trading Carbon Equivalent Units (Unidades de Carbono Equivalente - UCEs), representing verified emission reductions or removals equivalent to one ton of CO₂. Proponents must first reduce their emissions before compensating for any residuals via approved initiatives, such as forest conservation, renewable energy projects, or sustainable agricultural practices. The scheme ensures environmental and social safeguards, equitable benefit distribution, and alignment with national climate strategies, such as the REDD+ Action Plan and the National Climate Change Strategy.The Ministry of Environment, Water, and Ecological Transition (MAATE) oversees implementation through its Climate Change and Natural Heritage Subsecretariats, supported by accredited certification and verification bodies. It maintains a comprehensive registry for monitoring and tracking initiatives, UCEs, and compliance with program requirements. The system encourages transparency, additionality, and real, measurable outcomes that align with sustainable development goals while fostering multistakeholder collaboration across public and private sectors, Indigenous communities, and civil society.
Document Title: Ministerial Agreement No. MAATE-2023-053. Technical standard for Ecuador's Greenhouse Gas Emissions Compensation Scheme

Family Name: Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy
Family Summary: The Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy aims to guide national development in the long term, with a wide range of priority directions and quantified aims across sectors. It aims to reduce the carbon intensity of the economy (emissions per unit GDP) by 30% compared to 2010, increase renewables to 40% of generation, enhance energy efficiency, adapt public transport to green fuels, and establish an MRV system covering all greenhouse gases to support emissions trading. On the environment the strategy commits to the creation of 600,000 ha of green space, the reclamation of over 6000 ha of degraded mining land, and achieve essentially total spatial coverage of early warning systems for weather and flooding. It promotes research into climate-resilient high yielding crop varieties, and improved water management systems to adapt to increasing water scarcity.
Document Title: Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy

Family Name: Presidential Decree No. 06-2023 - Creation Of The National Policy To Prevent Deforestation And Forest Degradation
Family Summary: This decree establishes the National Policy aimed at preventing deforestation and forest degradation in the country. It outlines strategies and actions to protect forests, promote sustainable land management, and restore affected ecosystems. The policy focuses on addressing the main causes of deforestation and forest degradation, while involving various stakeholders, including local communities, governmental institutions, and the private sector, to ensure the preservation and sustainable use of forest resources.
Document Title: Presidential Decree No. 06-2023 - National Policy To Prevent Deforestation And Forest Degradation

Family Name: Memorandum No.5/1/2023-T&R (Mission on energy technologies)
Family Summary:
This Memorandum from the Ministry of Power and the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy sets up a Mission on Advanced and High-Impact Research (MAHIR) on the latest and emerging technologies in the energy sector. Th Mission will be for an initial period of five years, from 2023-2024 to 2027-28. The Mission is meant to support and provide funding for ideas to turn into products in the energy sector. Support will be in the form of identifying emerging technologies, supporting pilot projects for indigenous technologies, industrialising technologies, and leveraging foreign alliances and partnerships.

These are the eight areas identified for research: (1) alternatives to lithium-ion storage batteries; (2) modifying electric cookers/pans to suit Indian cooking methods; (3) green hydrogen for mobility (high efficiency fuel cell); (4) carbon capture); (5) geo-thermal energy; (6) solid state refrigeration; (7) nano technology for EV battery; and (8) indigenous CRGO technology.
Document Title: Memorandum No.5/1/2023-T&R (Mission on energy technologies)

Family Name: Decree no. 11.548/2023 establishing the National Comittee for REDD+
Family Summary:
This decree establishes the National Committee for the Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation, Conservation of Forest Carbon Stocks, Sustainable Management of Forests and Increase of Forest Carbon Stocks - REDD+.


This body is set up to provide guidance to state and federal governments and issue resolutions regarding the implementation of REDD+ in Brazil, in line with UNFCCC requirements. One of the Committee's responsibilities includes "the formulation, regulation and structuring of financial and market mechanisms to promote and encourage REDD+, pursuant to the provisions of art. 5th, art. 6th, art. 8 and art. 9 of Law No. 12,187, of December 29, 2009".


The decree sets out the mandate and composition of the Committee. The decree also revokes Decree No. 10.144, of November 28, 2019.
Document Title: Decree Nº 11.548 text

Family Name: Decree no. 11.550/2023 establishing the Interministerial Committee on Climate Change
Family Summary:
This decree institutes the Interministerial Committee on Climate Change as an institutional instrument of the federal Executive Branch to articulate government actions resulting from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change - UNFCCC, enacted by Decree No. 2652, of July 1, 1998, including the objective of neutrality climate change and any future subsidiary instruments.The decree sets out the responsibilities of the Committee, including providing guidance on the country’s climate change actions and proposing new sectoral programmes to be incorporated into the National Policy on Climate Change (PNMC). It also sets out the requirements for the membership and operation of the Committee. It also creates individual mandates for Ministries ranging from the Ministry of Finance to the Ministry of Environment with regard to climate action.The decree also revokes Decree No. 10,845, of October 25, 2021 and Decree No. 10,846, of October 25, 2021. The first of these Instituted an Interministerial Committee on Climate Change and Green Growth and the second Instituted a National Programme for Green Growth. It also revokes Decree No. 11.075, of May 19, 2022, which created a previous National System for the Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions (SINARE) and established the procedure for the elaboration of Sectorial Plans for Mitigation of Climate Changes. This Decree was updated by Decree 12.040/2024, which altered the provisions of some of its articles.

Resolution 6 of June 27, 2024 from the Inter Ministerial Committee on Climate Change (CIM) approves the Internal Regulations of the Inter Ministerial Committee on Climate Change (CIM). It defines the CIM’s Plenary composition and the purpose and components of the Subcommittee for COP 30, the Social Participation Chamber, the Interfederative Articulation Chamber and the Scientific Advisory Chamber, as well as providing for Technical Groups.
Document Title: Resolution 6, of June 27, 2024

Family Name: Low Carbon Development Strategy 2023-2030
Family Summary: This strategy examines and compares four business-as-usual scenarios and four mitigation scenarios, concluding that the most expensive scenario for the Republic of Serbia would be to ignore the costs related to climate change. Based on these results, the strategy seeks to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 13% by 2030 and 55% TO 69% by 2050 excluding land use, land use change, and forestry. It further aims to encourage the transition of the Republic of Serbia to a low-carbon and climate-resilient society.
Document Title: Low Carbon Development Strategy 2023-2030 with Projections until 2050

Family Name: Sector Action Plan on Environment and Climate Change
Family Summary:
The Action Plan outlines a strategic framework for integrating environmental sustainability and climate resilience into Bangladesh’s sectoral policies and programs. The Plan addresses pressing challenges such as deforestation, biodiversity loss, pollution, and climate change impacts, while advancing sustainable development goals across the Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock sectors by managing land, water, environment and ecosystem to achieve food and nutrition security. The Plan seeks to strengthen climate adaptation and mitigation efforts, build institutional capacity, and foster collaboration among stakeholders to address environmental and climate-related issues. It incorporates green technologies, sustainable resource management practices, and community-based approaches to enhance resilience and sustainability. The specific goals that the Action Plan seek to achieve include:

  • Promoting and enhancing local level climate change adaptation and resilience.
  • Development and expansion of Climate Smart Agriculture.
  • Promoting sustainable land and water management to achieve land degradation neutrality.
  • Environmental pollution control and conservation of ecosystem and biodiversity.
  • Promoting green growth and low carbon development.
  • Establishment of sustainable financing mechanism and strengthening institutions for environment and climate change risk management.
Document Title: Sector Action Plan on Environment and Climate Change

Family Name: Third Comprehensive Plan for Improvement of Carbon Sinks (2023-2027)
Family Summary: The 3rd Comprehensive Plan for Promoting Carbon Absorption Sources is set with the vision of 'contributing to the realisation of carbon neutrality and green growth through forests' and aims to 'contribute to 21% (30 million tons) of the national greenhouse gas reduction by 2027'. To realise this, 6 major promotion strategies and 20 key tasks have been discovered and presented.
Document Title: Third Comprehensive Plan for Improvement of Carbon Sinks

Family Name: Green Growth and Climate Resilience Strategy 2023
Family Summary: Rwanda's Green Growth and Climate Resilience Strategy from 2023 aims to support sustainable socioeconomic development, climate adaptation/resilience, and mitigation progress towards a goal for carbon neutrality by 2050. The strategy supports renewable energy development (including hydro, wind, solar), climate-smart dense urbanism, electrified and public transport. It also emphasises the need to enhance irrigation efficiency in the agricultural sector, improving climate resilience and rural income. For landscape-level resilience, the strategy promotes agroforestry and forest restoration.
Document Title: Green Growth and Climate Resilience Strategy 2023

Family Name: Advanced Technologies for Carbon-Neutral (ALCA-Next) Program
Family Summary: This program provides funding for promising research ideas in priority areas for carbon neutrality, with a budget of 1.6 billion yen for FY2024. The program was launched in 2023 under the Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST) as one of the JST Strategic Basic Research Programs. The program focuses on exploring challenging key technologies that have not been actively researched by industries but have the potential to become innovative technology game-changers. Initially, the program will adopt multiple projects with relatively smaller budgets for a "small start" phase lasting 3.5 years. After this period, approximately one-third of the projects will be selected through stage-gate evaluations to receive increased funding, ensuring a continuous funding stream for projects that pass the evaluation.
Document Title: Advanced Technologies for Carbon-Neutral (ALCA-Next) Program

Family Name: Blue Carbon Strategy
Family Summary: The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries established a 'Blue Carbon Promotion Strategy' with the aim of achieving the 2030 NDC and 2050 carbon-neutral goals. The blue carbon promotion strategy includes three strategies: 1) strengthening the ocean's carbon absorption capacity and climate disaster response ability; 2) expanding participation in blue carbon creation such as private, regional, and international cooperation; and 3) new blue carbon certification and laying a foundation for long-term promotion.
Document Title: Blue Carbon Strategy

Family Name: Decree 86/2023 on combating climate change
Family Summary:
This Decree's (pages 2179 to 2193 of the Gazette) objectives are as follows:

a) To strengthen the institutional framework for combating climate change, establish the responsibilities of the bodies and agencies of the Central State Administration, the business sector, the provincial governors of the People's Power and the municipal administration councils; of the State, the business sector, the provincial governors of the People's Power, and the municipal administration councils;

b) promote climate change adaptation and mitigation actions linked to food security, renewable energy use, energy efficiency, and integrated forest management, land use planning and urban planning instruments, cultural heritage, fisheries, agriculture, health, tourism, construction, transportation, and industry;

c) prioritise attention to climate change adaptation measures and disaster risk reduction management, with an emphasis on protecting people in vulnerable populations; land use planning and those resulting from the implementation of sectoral and coastal zone management policies;

d) strengthen mitigation actions, in accordance with the country's economic and social development priorities;

e) prioritise investments for the implementation of national measures and actions to address climate change in terms of mitigation and adaptation; and

f) promote scientific and technological training and innovation in line with climate change mitigation and adaptation actions.

This Decree contains provisions on the institutional framework for addressing climate change; the planning and orgaisation of government bodies; surveillance, early warning and assessment; the climate change information system; and the financing of actions to combat climate change and economic instruments.
Document Title: Decree 86/2023 on combating climate change

Family Name: Fifth Tourism Master Plan 2023-2027
Family Summary:
This Plan aims to strengthen Maldives’ position as a competitive and sustainable destination, enabling the industry,which has been the driving force in transforming the economy over the last 50 years, to continue leading the country’s growth. One of the goals is to build climate resilience and protect natural assets, which will be implemented through the following strategies:

  1. Improve planning guidelines and concept-approval processes to ensure sustainability is adequately addressed;
  2. Improve the management of common beach resources;
  3. Scale up and improve the quality of management systems to increase the resilience and health of coral reefs;
  4. Develop guidelines to ensure wildlife interactions are sustainable and in line with Maldives’ image and brand;
  5. Improve planning guidelines, knowledge sharing, and access to finance to adapt to climate change and build climate resilience into tourism infrastructure;
  6. Eliminate the use of single-use plastic products in tourist establishments in line with national targets;
  7. Reduce waste and develop and operationalise waste collection and processing infrastructure; and
  8. Develop a framework to renew and rejuvenate coconut palms and native vegetation.
Document Title: Fifth Tourism Master Plan 2023-2027

Family Name: Boursa Kuwait Capital Market Rules and Guidelines
Family Summary:
On May 22, 2023, the Capital Markets Authority (CMA), also known as "Boursa Kuwait” introduced new guidelines to help companies write their non-mandatory sustainability reports. 

These guidelines offer a starting point for companies to report on sustainability in ways that support Kuwait's goals for sustainable development as outlined in its Vision 2035 and its aim to have no net carbon emissions by 2060. The guidelines are based on international recommendations and are meant for all companies listed on Boursa Kuwait, but following them is not compulsory.

The guidelines suggest companies report on environmental issues like greenhouse gas emissions, energy and water use, and how they manage climate risks.
Document Title: Guidelines

Family Name: Zimbabwe National Forestry Policy 2023
Family Summary: The Zimbabwe National Forest Policy 2023 creates the framework for sustainable forest management to maintain biodiversity, productivity, regeneration capacity, and vitality. The policy aims “to enhance the contribution of the forestry sector to development and social equity through active participation of all stakeholders for the benefit of present and future generations.” Regarding climate change, the policy has an objective to “enhance forest carbon sinks and build communities’ resilience to climate change through sustainable forest management.” It proposes policy actions such as promoting land-use plans that recognise forestry at all governance levels, capacity building for sustainable forest management in the context of climate change, maintaining and accounting for carbon sinks with community participation, implementing a carbon credit framework as a guide in forest-based projects and promote gender-sensitive forest-based climate solutions.
Document Title: Zimbabwe National Forestry Policy 2023

Family Name: The Swedish Environmental Protection Agency's Action Plan for Climate Adaptation 2023–2026
Family Summary:
One of the main focuses of the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency's climate adaptation work is to spread knowledge and strengthen incentives for work with nature-based solutions.

Action objectives:

• The Swedish Environmental Protection Agency is based on nature's ability to contribute to reducing negative effects of a changing climate through nature-based solutions through measures that simultaneously strengthen biodiversity and promote human well-being.

• The Swedish Environmental Protection Agency's climate adaptation work shall contribute to the implementation of the Swedish Climate Act - to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases by preserving, managing and creating new functions in the environment.

• Climate adaptation is an integral part of the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency's acquisition and property management of state property, in the protection and management of protected areas and in the coordination and development of outdoor life issues.

• The Swedish Environmental Protection Agency shall, through environmental monitoring and environmental analysis, work to ensure that changes in species and ecosystems as a result of a changing climate can be detected and explained.

• Climate adaptation is integrated into the application of the Environmental Code through planning, assessment and supervision.
Document Title: The Swedish Environmental Protection Agency's Action Plan for Climate Adaptation 2023–2026

Family Name: Long-term Strategy on Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reductions
Family Summary:
This Strategy sets out sector-specific and technology pathways to reaching Ireland's 2050 climate targets.


A key objective of the Strategy is to clarify sectoral adjustments required to reach net zero by 2050 and support policy stability and investment in the medium- and long-term.


The Strategy contains measures categorised according to the degree of certainty around their use and suitability to realise 2030 and 2050 targets.


Core measures include technologies and measures that already exist today and could deliver substantial emissions reduction. Those focus on delivering a renewable electricity system; GHG-efficient agricultural practices; electrification in transport, built environment, and industry; restoration of forestry and peatlands; fuel substitution; and a circular economy.


Further measures are those technologies and measures that are technologically more challenging or not yet available at scale but required to deliver the climate targets. Such measures are aimed at accelerating a sustainable transformation in agriculture and deploy zero-emission gas.


Alternative-further measures are those technologies which currently exist at research or pilot stage or have not reached commercial scale, such as radical demand reduction (e.g. aviation) and deploy carbon capture and storage in the industry sector.
Document Title: Long-term Strategy on Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reductions

Family Name: Directive on Mandatory Reporting on Greenhouse Gases
Family Summary: The Directive on Mandatory Reporting on Greenhouse Gases aims to enhance national monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) of greenhouse gas emissions and removals, forming a robust carbon accounting framework to guide future efforts such as nationally determined contributions. This directive begins the process of creating a national carbon inventory, and sets out the basic responsibilities of the Brunei Climate Change Secretariat to do so.
Document Title: Directive on Mandatory Reporting on Greenhouse Gases

Family Name: Security Strategy for the Kingdom of the Netherlands (De Veiligheidsstrategie voor het Koninkrijk der Nederlanden)
Family Summary:
Outside of national safety concerning the geopolitical balance of power and instability, as well as in today’s digital world, this report includes the security strategy for “a ready and resilient society” to protect national security from climate and natural disasters, and the potential impact of climate change. Specifically for the Netherlands, it discusses the risk of drought, and wildfires, whereas for the Caribbean part of the Kingdom it discusses the threat of hurricanes and its consequences potentially being even greater if critical infrastructure and other processes are protected. It also refers to the rise in sea levels posing a significant threat to the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Moreover, it discusses the social tension that may arise from the increasing inequality or fundamentally different views on how to address climate change and the energy transition. 

Line of Action 9 discusses the need to intensify climate mitigation and adaptation, and discusses the priorities for 2023-2029, below discussed in short:  

A. Achieve climate mitigation goals and reduce international footprint

B. Increase the urgency of the implementation of national and international climate plans and agreements

C. Ensure that the Netherlands is fully circular by 2050

D. Ensure security of supply for critical materials needed for the energy and digital transitions

E. Take into account the risks to national security in the area of spatial planning

F. Strengthen the approach to wildfire prevention

G. Define a long-term approach to the effects of climate change for the Caribbean part of the Kingdom

H. Take climate risks and resilience into account in strategic and security policy

I. Disseminate Dutch knowledge regarding climate vulnerability and risk assessment, and stress the importance of following a conflict-sensitive approach in climate efforts

J. Contribute to greater water security and water safety in fragile states
Document Title: Report on the Security Strategy for the Kingdom of the Netherlands

Family Name: Second Transitional National Development Plan
Family Summary:
This two-year Transitional National Development Plan (TNDP), with the theme “Towards a High-Income Economy: Transformation Now, Prosperity Tomorrow”, builds on other initiatives aimed at catapulting the country onto a path of socioeconomic progress towards 2036. The Plan outlines the national priorities, strategies, programmes and projects. It offers an opportunity to transition and institutionalise the necessary reforms into the planning system, laying a firm foundation for future Development Plans. This Plan contains actions on the development of climate-smart agriculture, climate change-resilient society, and green growth through reforms in the power sector.

The TNDP has identified eight key policy priorities to be pursued during its lifespan. The priorities were developed taking into account the global and domestic macroeconomic developments, the Reset Agenda, and the desire to achieve high growth status, among others. Family Name: International Climate Finance Strategy 2023
Family Summary:
The UK International Climate Finance Strategy sets out how the government will deliver on its pledge to double its International Climate Finance (ICF) commitments to £11.6bn between 2021 and 2026, including at least £3bn on development solutions that protect and restore nature. The provision of ICF will be balanced between support for mitigation and adaptation measures. Over the five year period covered by the Strategy, the UK’s ICF will be spread across four key themes: 

1. Reducing global reliance on fossil fuels by supporting the acceleration of the transition to clean energy in energy-producing and energy-consuming sectors;

2. The protection, sustainable management and restoration of nature by ensuring that the global financial and economic systems tackle unattainable production and consumption, through supporting governments, central banks, businesses and financial institutions to integrate the value of nature into decision-making processes;

3. Building the capacity of people and communities to adapt and become more resilient to the impacts of climate change, supporting the transformation of systems, and helping countries and communities to address impacts when they occur; and

4. Supporting low-carbon, green and resilient urbanisation to promote sustainable and accessible cities, as well as enabling access to clean and reliable infrastructure.


The Strategy is published alongside Powering Up Britain, including the Net Zero Growth and Energy Security Plans, the 2023 Been Finance Strategy, and the UK’s 2030 Strategy Framework for Climate and Nature Action and collectively form the UK’s response to driving progress on addressing climate change.

Family Name: Carbon Markets Rules for the Kingdom of Bhutan 2023
Family Summary:
The 2023 Carbon Markets Rules for the Kingdom of Bhutan provides guidance on how Bhutan will facilitate its participation in cooperative approaches with other parties to the Paris Agreement under Article 6.2.The rules are applicable to all activities within Bhutan that seek to participate in either compliance or voluntary carbon markets, specifically for the issuance of a Letter of Authorisation to facilitate corresponding adjustments. For activities of the voluntary market that do not require a Letter of Authorisation, entities do not need to obtain approval, as these activities do not impact Bhutan’s international climate commitments.

Institutional Arrangements

  • National Climate Change Committee (NCCC): This high-level committee sets the overall scope for Article 6 engagement and approves fees for corresponding adjustments.
  • Climate Change Coordination Committee (C4): This committee reviews and develops methodologies, oversees technical guidelines, and proposes activities eligible for carbon market participation for NCCC approval. It also sets technical standards, accredits third-party auditors, and handles the certification and issuance of emission reduction credits. C4 is responsible for authorising projects and participants to generate and transact Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs), and managing grievances and appeals.
  • Department of Environment and Climate Change (DECC): The DECC defines the carbon asset development process, accredits auditors, registers projects, and certifies emission reductions. It also proposes project authorisations for generating and transacting ITMOs, sets fees for corresponding adjustments, and executes the transfer of Article 6 units. Additionally, the DECC carries out corresponding adjustments and reports on projects and transfers in the Biennial Transfer Reports for Article 6 Technical Expert Review.

Process

  • Participation requirement: Entities must obtain a Letter of Authorisation from the DECC.
  • Validation and verification: Mitigation activities need to be validated and verified according to procedures established by the National Environment Commission (NEC).
  • Authorisation details: Once authorised, entities can manage, sell, and transfer any mitigation outcomes arising from the authorised activities, in accordance with the conditions set in the Letter of Authorisation.
  • Payment for corresponding adjustments: The DECC specifies the payment required for corresponding adjustments at the time of granting the Letter of Authorisation.
Document Title: Carbon Markets Rules for the Kingdom of Bhutan 2023

Family Name: National Carbon Market Framework
Family Summary:
Rwanda's national carbon market framework details the administrative and institutional framework for Article 6 implementation, as well as the guiding principles to facilitate Rwanda's participation in carbon markets both within and outside Article 6 (6.2 6.4) and in non-market approaches under Article 6.8.

Administrative and Institutional Framework

The institutional framework consists of an Extended Governing Board (Oversight Body) and an Article 6 Unit.

1) Oversight Body

The Oversight Body provides long-term oversight of adopting necessary legislation and institutional mandates for the support of Article 6 activities. Its responsibilities include:

  • Coordination among multiple ministries.
  • Advising on Article 6 participation strategy.
  • Monitoring of the implementation of the framework.
  • Coordination with other climate and sectoral initiatives.

2) Article 6 Unit

The Article 6 Unit, also known as the carbon market office, is tasked with defining and implementing the Article 6 Framework. It is responsible for:

  • Operationalizing activities;
  • Managing the share of proceeds;
  • Providing technical support;
  • Overseeing transparency and accounting requirements, including recording and reporting activities and managing corresponding adjustments;
  • Developing and implementing procedures to facilitate the country's participation in the framework, which includes:
    • Identifying eligible mitigation activities;
    • Establishing authorisation and approval mechanisms;
    • Verifying and issuing Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs);
    • Applying corresponding adjustments;
    • Integrating reporting and accounting into the national system for reporting to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).

3) Designated National Authority

The Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA), previously the Designated National Authority (DNA) for the CDM has been designated as the focal point for Article 6.4.

Policy Framework and Guiding Principles

Rwanda's guidelines for participation are in line with provisions of the Paris Agreement, and come with additional specifications for Rwanda's case. The framework mentions that the Government of Rwanda approves Article 6.2 activities and Article 6.4 projects based on national interest, and activities seeking recognition as non-market approaches require approval, and offset projects in the voluntary market need a letter of no-objection. Voluntary market projects labelled as Article 6 will imply the contribution of a share of proceeds (which can be thought of as a tax on market mechanisms) for the administration of carbon markets provision. There will also be special attention paid to forestry sector projects under Article 6, which will have to adhere to Law n47bis/2013 on the sale of forestry services.

Share of Proceeds Fees

A share of proceeds will apply for the approval of Article 6 activities, and the issuance of a letter of no objection for voluntary market projects. However, the level of share of proceeds is yet to be determined.

  • Develop capacities and technologies to enhance adaptation and mitigation to effects of climate change.

Family Name: CAP Strategic Plan 2023–2027
Family Summary:
Wallonia – CAP Strategic Plan 2023–2027

The Walloon CAP Strategic Plan 2023–2027 is designed to strengthen the economic resilience of farms while accelerating the environmental and climate transition of the agricultural sector. The plan supports a broad range of farming systems, including conventional, organic, livestock and arable production, and combines income support with rural development measures. Key priorities include improving farm competitiveness, encouraging generational renewal through dedicated support for young farmers, promoting cooperation and innovation, and increasing the use of digital technologies in agriculture and rural areas. Environmental objectives are integrated through eco-schemes and agri-environmental measures aimed at biodiversity protection, climate mitigation and sustainable land management. Wallonia’s plan forms part of the EU’s reformed Common Agricultural Policy and was approved by the European Commission for implementation during the 2023–2027 period.

Flanders – CAP Strategic Plan 2023–2027The Flemish CAP Strategic Plan 2023–2027 (Vlaams GLB-Strategisch Plan) sets out how Flanders implements the EU Common Agricultural Policy to achieve its economic, environmental and social objectives. The plan combines Pillar I measures—including direct income support and sectoral interventions for fruit, vegetables and beekeeping—with Pillar II rural development measures, which replace the previous Rural Development Programme (PDPO). A key feature of the Flemish strategy is its strengthened green architecture, integrating conditionality, eco-schemes, agri-environment-climate measures and management agreements to promote climate action, biodiversity conservation and the sustainable management of natural resources. The plan also supports farm competitiveness, innovation, knowledge transfer and generational renewal, while transferring part of the Pillar I budget to Pillar II to reinforce investments in rural development and environmental measures. The European Commission approved the Flemish CAP Strategic Plan on 5 December 2022, with subsequent amendments updating its implementation from 2024 onwards.

Family Name: The UK Government Resilience Framework
Family Summary:
The UK Government Resilience Framework (2022) sets out a long-term approach to strengthening the UK’s ability to anticipate, prevent, prepare for, respond to and recover from a wide range of risks, including the increasing impacts of climate change. It establishes three core principles: developing a shared understanding of risks, prioritising prevention and preparation over response alone, and treating resilience as a “whole of society” responsibility. Climate change is identified as a chronic and interconnected risk requiring greater consideration of long-term vulnerabilities, including impacts on critical infrastructure, supply chains, communities and public services. The Framework establishes a plan to 2030 focused on strengthening risk assessment, government responsibilities, partnerships, community resilience, investment and skills, and complements dedicated climate adaptation policies such as the National Adaptation Programme.

The December 2023 update reports progress in implementing the Framework, including new processes for identifying chronic risks such as climate change, and greater focus on interconnected risks and critical infrastructure.

Family Name: Decree No 2022 - 698
Family Summary:
Decree No. 2022-698 establishes the procedures for registering carbon projects within the country. The Autorité d'Enregistrement des Projets Carbone (AEPC), or Carbon Project Registration Authority, is the government institution responsible for overseeing the implementation of this decree. The AEPC's mission includes promoting carbon projects, ensuring compliance with relevant norms and standards, and facilitating the registration and monitoring of these projects.

Project registration

All new carbon project developers in Benin must submit a registration request to the Autorité d’Enregistrement at least three weeks before submitting their validation report to a greenhouse gas certification program or relevant carbon standard. The request must include all required documentation for review.

Projects already certified or in the certification process when the decree was adopted must apply for registration within two months of its adoption.

The project document submitted for validation must include the following elements:

- Project description and development timeline

- Geographic area covered by the project

- Chosen greenhouse gas certification program or carbon standard

- Applied methodology

- Identification of stakeholders, including local communities, investors, and project developers

- Description of economic and social co-benefits

- Estimated greenhouse gas reductions and removals during the crediting period

- Proof of property rights or agreements with property owners related to the mitigation activity

- Stakeholder consultation details, including consent from local populations and communities

- Government authorizations, including environmental impact assessments and permits, if necessary

- Demonstration of project alignment with the Paris Agreement, Benin's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), and relevant goals.

Carbon rights

- Beninese citizens, communities, and registered entities have the right to participate in the carbon market, including proposing and developing projects.

- All carbon credits generated by projects in Benin are sovereign assets.

- The state can assign or transfer carbon rights to private developers.

- The terms for transferring or conceding carbon rights will be set by a decree from the Minister of Finance, based on a proposal from the Autorité d'Enregistrement.

Participation in Article 6

- The government of Benin decides, at its discretion, to participate in mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to achieve emission reduction and other sustainable environmental goals.

- Private entities may be authorized to participate in these mechanisms after approval, based on criteria and guarantees set by the government.

- Emission reductions from carbon projects in Benin will contribute to the country’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).

- The government will assess scenarios for applying corresponding adjustments in line with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, including relevant procedures, rules, and conditions.
Document Title: Decree No 2022 - 698

Family Name: Nature Positive Plan: better for the environment, better for business
Family Summary:
This Plan sets out the Australian government’s commitment to reform Australia’s environmental laws to better protect, restore and manage our unique environment.

The government supports the recommendation of the review that proponents be required to publish their expected Scope 1 and 2 emissions. Further, proponents will be required to disclose how their project aligns with Australia’s national and international obligations to reduce emissions. The changing climate will also be a mandatory consideration in environmental planning approaches. Improvements in information and guidance will support these reforms.

The government recognises the risks global warming poses to Australia’s unique ecosystems and the link between climate and biodiversity. They will address this by embedding climate considerations in all roles and functions of government. In addition to their commitments to reduce national emissions to 43% below 2005 levels by 2030, and to achieve net zero emissions by 2050, the government will integrate climate change considerations, where relevant, throughout national environmental law without duplicating existing mechanisms for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. This includes improved transparency in project assessments; improved planning and landscape-scale approaches to facilitate adaptation to climate change; and improved information and climate-impact modelling.
Document Title: Nature Positive Plan: better for the environment, better for business

Family Summary: The Agriculture and Rural Development 2023-2027 strategic plan aims to achieve stable development of Lithuania's food production and rural land, guiding the deployment of domestic policy and EU funding, and names contributing to climate goals among its main priorities. Climate adaptation measures in the plan emphasise the importance of widespread efficiency improvements to irrigation systems. The plan also contains significant measures for forest restoration; reconfiguration of crop systems to reverse declines in agricultural soil carbon storage across Lithuania; biogas installation and development; and funding for research, innovation and more general capacity-building.

Family Name: Germany’s CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027
Family Summary: Germany's CAP Strategic Plan (GAP-Strategieplan) implements the EU's Common Agricultural Policy for the 2023–2027 funding period, combining both CAP pillars into a single national plan: Pillar 1 direct payments (including the voluntary "Öko-Regelungen," rewarding farmers for additional environmental services such as arable land set-aside, grassland extensification, or agroforestry) and Pillar 2 targeted programmes for sustainable land management and rural development. Covering roughly €30 billion in EU funding over the period and directly addressing over 300,000 applicants in the agricultural sector, the plan was developed in close coordination with federal ministries, the federal states, and economic, environmental, and social partners. It was initially approved by the European Commission on 21 November 2022 (Version 1.0); the currently valid version is 7.1, approved by the European Commission on 9 December 2025. More than half of EU funds under the plan are now directed toward environmental and climate objectives, positioning it as Germany's key implementing instrument contributing to the EU's Green Deal, Biodiversity Strategy, and Farm to Fork Strategy.
Document Title: Germany’s CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027 - Summary

Family Name: National Peatland Conservation Strategy (Nationale Moorschutzstrategie)
Family Summary: The strategy supports Germany's goal of achieving climate neutrality by 2045. Its measures aim to reduce annual greenhouse gas emissions from peat soils by at least 5 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent by 2030. Currently, more than 90% of Germany's moorlands are drained to the point of emitting roughly 53 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent annually, and peat soils represent Germany's largest terrestrial carbon store. The strategy centers on rewetting drained moors and peat soils, alongside climate-compatible long-term use of these areas, while also aiming to strengthen biodiversity in moorland regions.

Family Name: National REDD+ Strategy
Family Summary: Pakistan's National REDD+ Strategy aims to provide a set of policies, actions and measures to restore forests nationally, decreasing net emissions and improving resilience to climate threats while allowing sustainable livelihoods for those dependent on forestry resources. It promotes several strategy options for implementation: reforestation/restoration/afforestation; sustainable forest management; payment for ecosystem services; silvo-pastoral/agroforestry practices; and sustainable/eco tourism. The strategy names synergies and barriers for these strategy options in its implementation framework, and then gives strategic policies/measures alongside a roadmap. It calls for addressing land tenure conflicts. strengthening institutional capacity, strengthening legal structures, improving cross-sectoral co-ordination, promoting public/stakeholder awareness, and the mainstreaming of gender in forest/REDD+ policy.

Family Name: National REDD+ Strategy
Family Summary: Gabon's National REDD+ Strategy aims to facilitate the sustainable management and restoration of forest resources, preserving their role in carbon sequestration to mitigate climate change while preserving rural livelihoods. It promotes increased efficiency of existing agriculture, allowing land-sparing, and the creation of timber plantations in already-degraded areas, reducing the impact on primary forest. It aims to introduce and enhance forest certifications, allowing better monitoring and funding by international carbon markets, and to increase forest-sector revenues by increasing the domestic processing of wood before export. The strategy also aims to improve enforcement of laws around logging and forest use, build general institutional capacity, and promote sustainable eco-tourism.

Family Name: Climate Strategy 2050
Family Summary:
This document sets out Liechtenstein's climate strategy to 2050. This includes:

  • Reaching net zero by 2050;
  • By 2030, 50% GHG emissions reduction compared to 1990 levels. 40% are to be reduced domestically, 10% abroad; and
  • By 2050, reduce domestic emissions by 90% compared to 1990 levels. The remaining 10% are to be compensated.

The Strategy prioritises the energy sector. Compared to 1990 levels, emissions must be reduced by 50% by 2030, and completely by 2050. 

For the compensation of remaining emissions, the Strategy mentions carbon sinks such as forests and moors. It further announces monitoring the development of negative emissions technologies.

Lastly, the Strategy touches on emissions abroad which are to be reduced as well.

  • The climate protection contribution of forest and wood is maintained and expanded;
  • The use of wood from domestic forestry is expanded;
  • Establish a model for the remuneration of climate protection services;
  • Wind turbines in the forest contribute to the energy supply;
  • Implement action plans for the adaptation of forests;
  • Strengthen forest conversion;
  • Support measures for the adaptation of forests and for forest conversion; and
  • Establish monitoring of climate change.
Document Title: Forest Strategy 2050

Family Name: Cabinet of Ministers Regulation No. 675/2022 on GHG inventory, projections and adaptation to climate change reporting system
Family Summary:
‘Regulation No. 675 defines the procedures for creating and maintaining the National Greenhouse Gas Inventory System and the Forecasting System. It outlines the specific responsibilities of various institutions in gathering activity data and emission factors. Its aim is to ensure that all data regarding pollution, carbon capture, and future forecasts are accurate, transparent, and compliant with international treaty obligations by outlining:

  1. the procedure for the establishment and maintenance of a national system for the preparation of an inventory of greenhouse gases;
  2. the procedures for the establishment and maintenance of the national greenhouse gas forecasting system; and
  3. the procedures for establishing and maintaining a national system for reporting on adaptation to climate change.

Family Name: Regulation 21/2022 on Guidelines for Implementing the Carbon Economic Value
Family Summary:
In order to support the achievement of Indonesia’s NDC greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets and to implement the provisions of Presidential Regulation Number 98 of 2021 on the Implementation of Carbon Pricing to Achieve the Nationally Determined Contribution Target and Control Over Greenhouse Gas Emissions in National Development, this Regulation introduces the procedure for implementing carbon pricing in Indonesia. Carbon pricing applies to the following sectors: energy; waster; industrial processes and product uses; agriculture; forestry; and other sectors in accordance with developments in science and technology. The implementation of the carbon pricing is carried out through the following mechanisms: carbon trading; result-based payments; and carbon levies, as well as other mechanisms that accord with developments in science and technology. Carbon trading may be carried out through domestic and international trading procedures. The Regulation sets out the provisions of a Carbon Trading Roadmap, which carbon trading activities must comply with, and establishes the rules for offsetting GHG emissions from activities that are either uncapped or do not meet the sectoral GHG Emission Baseline.

The Regulation further outlines the procedures for Result-Based Payments and the Carbon Levy.
Document Title: Regulation 21/2022

Family Name: The Netherlands' Global Climate Strategy (Internationale Klimaatstrategie)
Family Summary:
This is the first “whole-of-government” Global Climate Strategy that describes how the Netherlands wants to strengthen their response to the challenges that climate change poses, both domestically and globally. It's centred around four topics: 1) adaptation 2) mitigation 3) finance 4) loss and damage.

Adaptation: In order to reduce climate change vulnerability worldwide the Netherlands will

  • Double their adaptation finance (in line with the Glasgow Climate Pact)
  • Co-host the UN 2023 Water Conference
  • Provide an additional EUR 250 million until 2025 to increase accessibility to food in regions that are climate-vulnerable
  • Share Dutch knowledge and expertise on water management, the adaptation policy cycle, and smarter food production

Mitigation: Centred around helping the acceleration to a net-zero circular economy by 2050 globally

  • Raising its national target for CO2 reduction to at least 55%, with policies focused on pursuing of 60% reduction 
  • Focus on partnerships with other countries to support net-zero ambitions
  • Speed up the transition to zero-emission mobility and transport
  • Cooperate with relevant actors (civil society, financial and knowledge institutions, environmental organisations etc)
  • Double the financial contribution to stopping deforestation

Finance

  • Increase climate finance with more than EUR 0.5 billion a year
  • Develop instruments to mobilise more private capital for climate action in developing countries
  • Partner for clean energy transition
  • Strengthen sustainable investment, fighting greenwashing, and enhance the transparency in climate risks and impact

Loss and damage

  • Increase the support to disaster risk management, with a special focus on universally available early warning systems and capacity to act
Document Title: The Netherlands’ Global Climate Strategy

Family Name: National Adaptation Plan of Bangladesh (2023-2050)
Family Summary:
The National Adaptation Plan (NAP) of Bangladesh (2023–2050) presents a long-term vision for enhancing climate resilience across all sectors of the economy. It outlines priority actions to reduce climate vulnerabilities, protect ecosystems, and assist communities in adapting to the impacts of climate change. The overall goal of the plan is to build a climate-resilient nation through effective adaptation strategies that foster a strong society, support ecosystems, and promote sustainable economic growth. The NAP integrates adaptation measures into national planning processes and encourages sustainable practices to protect essential sectors, including agriculture, water resources, health, and infrastructure. The following goals are established:

1. Ensure protection against climate change variability and induced natural disasters.

2. Develop climate-resilient agriculture to secure food, nutrition, and livelihoods.

3. Create climate-smart cities to enhance the urban environment and overall well-being.

4. Promote nature-based solutions for the conservation of forestry, biodiversity, and community well-being.

5. Strengthen governance by integrating adaptation strategies into planning processes.

6. Foster transformative capacity-building and innovation for climate change adaptation.

The principles guiding the NAP include: recognizing that priority sectors are interconnected and require a multidisciplinary approach; ensuring that the NAP process is driven by the country’s needs and is participatory, inclusive, and gender-sensitive; promoting nature-based solutions; engaging the private sector; and maintaining financial integrity through effective monitoring, evaluation, and learning.
Document Title: National Adaptation Plan of Bangladesh (2023-2050)

Family Name: National Strategy for Digital Agriculture in Niger and its Action Plan (2023-2027)
Family Summary:
The National Strategy for Digital Agriculture in Niger (2023–2035) aims to harness digital technologies to strengthen food security and rural livelihoods through a sustainable transformation of the agricultural sector. Its vision emphasizes climate-resilient agriculture by ensuring the sustainable use of rural ecosystems, supporting efficient production systems, improving value chains, and expanding access to diversified food products. The strategy identifies four overarching objectives that align with Niger’s broader development agenda: sustainable management of agricultural ecosystems, improved agronomic and environmental performance of farms, stronger agricultural value chains, and increased use of digital services by rural communities.

To achieve these goals, the 2023–2027 Action Plan outlines six priority areas, many of which directly address climate change adaptation and resilience. These include deploying digital tools for preserving ecosystems, biodiversity, soils, and water resources; supporting secure land and pastoral management in the context of growing pressures on natural resources; and promoting efficient, climate-smart production systems that strengthen food and nutrition security. The plan also emphasises building rural actors’ digital skills, improving access to information and services, and enhancing market opportunities. Overall, this strategy will reinforce the country's capacity to adapt to climate change while fostering inclusive rural development.
Document Title: National Strategy for Digital Agriculture and its Action Plan (2023-2027)

Family Name: Carbon Neutral Finland 2035: National Climate and Energy Strategy
Family Summary:
The primary goal of the strategy is to achieve carbon neutrality by 2035. It outlines the measures Finland will implement to meet the European Union’s climate commitments for 2030 and the targets set in the Climate Change Act, including a 60 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2035.

The strategy addresses all greenhouse gas emissions across various sectors, including the emissions trading sector, the effort-sharing sector, and the land use sector. It also considers carbon sinks within the land use sector and other areas. The strategy encompasses the five dimensions of the EU’s Energy Union: decarbonisation of the economy, renewable energy, energy efficiency, internal energy market, energy security, and the promotion of research, innovation, and competitiveness.

Key provisions in the strategy include:

1. Utilising the emissions trading system as a key instrument to reduce emissions.

2. Integrating climate and energy policies to ensure a cohesive approach.

3. Involving various stakeholders, including businesses, communities, and government agencies, in the implementation of the strategy.

4. Establishing mechanisms for monitoring progress and reporting on the implementation of the strategy.

This strategy updated and strengthened Finland's energy and climate policy framework, reflecting the legally binding 2035 carbon-neutrality target, EU climate objectives and the need to accelerate the clean transition. It covers the energy, transport, buildings, industry, agriculture and land-use sectors and places particular emphasis on renewable energy, energy efficiency, electrification, energy security and reducing dependence on fossil fuels. The strategy also responds to the energy-market disruption caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Document Title: Carbon neutral Finland 2035 - national climate and energy strategy

Family Name: Finland’s CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027
Family Summary: The new CAP period from 2023 to 2027 began in January 2023. The main tasks of Finland's CAP Strategic Plan (CSP) include safeguarding active food production, climate and environmental sustainability in agriculture and strengthening the vitality of regenerating rural areas. In its CAP strategic plan, each EU country is obliged to display a higher ambition on environment and climate action compared to the previous programming period. Each country is also required to update the plan when climate and environmental legislation is modified. The aim is that 40 per cent of the total EU funding for CAP measures will be allocated to climate measures at the EU level. Member States are obliged to allocate 35 per cent of the rural development funds to environmental and climate measures at the national level. In addition to this, at least 25 per cent of the budget for direct payments is allocated to eco-schemes, providing stronger incentives for climate- and environment-friendly farming practices and approaches.Key targets include reducing agricultural greenhouse-gas emissions, improving nutrient management, protecting biodiversity, supporting sustainable farming practices, and strengthening rural businesses and communities. The plan also promotes knowledge, innovation and digitalisation in agriculture and rural areas. Its national objectives are assessed against the 2022 baseline, with targets set primarily for 2027.
Document Title: CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027
