Family Name: Peru's National Territorial Planning Strategy (Estrategia Nacional de Ordenamiento Territorial)
Family Summary: The "National Strategy for Territorial Planning of Sedatu 2020-2040" in Mexico aims to shape the spatial dimension of the country's development over the long term. It acknowledges the negative impacts of past urbanisation and housing policies, including increased regional inequalities, disordered urban sprawl, exploitation of natural resources, and ecosystem degradation. The strategy emphasises that climate change and inequality are critical challenges, and decisions regarding cities, territories, and resource use will have global consequences. Territorial Planning is presented as a public policy to reduce social inequalities, build more sustainable, safe, and inclusive settlements, and promote rational natural resource use.The strategy prioritises social-spatial justice, focusing on vulnerable groups and indigenous communities, ensuring safe environments with climate change adaptation capabilities. It seeks to strengthen climate change mitigation and adaptation measures, promote rational land use, and conserve ecosystem services for balanced, sustainable development across all regions. Key challenges addressed include promoting clean energy sources, fulfilling international commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and implementing sustainable waste management practices. The strategy also aims to reduce social vulnerability to disasters, improve basic services in urban and rural areas, and strengthen the capacity of municipalities to adapt to disaster risks related to natural phenomena by 2040.
Document Title: Peru's National Strategy for Territorial Planning of Sedatu (Estrategia Nacional de Ordenamiento Territorial de la Sedatu)

Family Name: Internal Organic Regulations of the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Reglamento Orgánico Interno del Ministerio de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales)
Family Summary: Government Agreement No. 73-2021 establishes the organic structure and functions of Guatemala's Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (MARN), with particular emphasis on climate change governance and environmental management. The regulation reorganises MARN to enhance implementation of environmental policies, including conservation, protection, and improvement of environmental resources, while specifically incorporating climate change adaptation, mitigation, and vulnerability reduction as core ministerial functions. The framework aligns with Guatemala's international environmental obligations and domestic legislation, including the Climate Change Adaptation and Greenhouse Gas Mitigation Law (Decree No. 7-2013).The restructuring creates a dedicated Vice-Ministry for Natural Resources and Climate Change, comprising specialised departments for climate vulnerability and adaptation, mitigation strategies, climate science and metrics, risk prevention, and land degradation control. This institutional framework establishes systematic approaches to greenhouse gas monitoring, climate data integration, and multi-sectoral coordination for climate action. The regulation mandates development of climate adaptation and mitigation strategies, implementation of the national climate change information system, and coordination of international climate commitments, including reporting under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, thereby institutionalising climate governance within Guatemala's environmental administration.
Document Title: Government Agreement 73-2021 (Acuerdo Gubernativo 73-2021)

Family Name: Czechia's recovery and resilience plan
Family Summary:
To benefit from the support of the Recovery and Resilience Facility set up by the EU in the aftermath of the COVID-19-induced economic crisis, Member States submit their recovery and resilience plans to the European Commission. Each plan sets out the reforms and investments to be implemented by end-2026 and Member States can receive financing up to a previously agreed allocation. Each plan should effectively address challenges identified in the European Semester, particularly the country-specific recommendations of 2019 and 2020 adopted by the Council. It should also advance the green and digital transitions and make Member States’ economies and societies more resilient. The Commission validates the plan after which it effectively enters in force and EU subsidies can start flowing towards the member state.The European Commission has given a positive assessment to Czechia’s recovery and resilience plan, which will be financed by €7 billion in grants. 42% of the plan’s total allocation for reforms and investments supports climate objectives, including:

  • Energy efficiency: financing large-scale renovation programmes to increase the energy efficiency of residential and public buildings, childcare and long-term care facilitites. €1.6 billion
  • Renewable energy sources: supporting the installation of renewable energy sources for businesses and households. €480 million
  • Sustainable mobility: financing of more than 5,000 low-emission vehicles for the public and business sector, promoting the deployment of over 4,500 electric charging stations, improving railway infrastructure and 90 km of cycling pathways. €1.1 billion
  • Circular economy: investing in recycling infrastructure and support for circular economy solutions and water savings in businesses.€141 million

Czechia’s recovery and resilience plan was updated on 17 October 2023 also to introduce a REPowerEU chapter. It outlines:

  • 105 investment streams and 58 reforms
  • 43% of the plan will support climate objectives
  • 23% of the plan will foster the digital transition.

The reforms address bottlenecks to lasting and sustainable growth, while investments are targeted to accelerate the transition towards low-carbon and climate-resilient economy, to maximise the benefits of the digital transformation and improve the quality of public administration. The plan also aims at fostering social cohesion and resilience by increasing the availability and quality of healthcare, tackling inequalities in education and investing in pre-school facilities. All measures have to be implemented within a tight time frame, as the Regulation establishing the Recovery and Resilience Facility requires all milestones and targets within the national plans to be completed by August 2026.
Document Title: Government resolution 957/2023 established the consolidated version of the Recovery Plan

Each plan sets out the reforms and investments to be implemented by end-2026 and Member States can receive financing up to a previously agreed allocation. Each plan should effectively address challenges identified in the European Semester, particularly the country-specific recommendations of 2019 and 2020 adopted by the Council. It should also advance the green and digital transitions and make Member States’ economies and societies more resilient.The Total value reaches approx. €59.8 billion, which are divided into (i) €25.3 billion in RRF grants and (ii) €34.5 billion in RRF loans.

Poland’s plan strongly supports climate and environment objectives:

• ≈46.6 % of funding goes to green projects.

• Includes investment in renewable energy (offshore onshore wind), energy-efficient building renovations, green hydrogen, and sustainable transport.

• Regulatory changes to facilitate renewable projects and electricity imports.

The plan was approved by the Council on 17 June 2022.
Document Title: Poland’s Recovery and Resilience Plan

Family Name: Decision no. 523/QD-TTg on approving the Viet Nam’s Forestry Development Strategy in the 2021-2030 period, with a vision to 2050
Family Summary:
The general objectives of this Strategy is to build the forestry into an economic-technical sector and maximise the potentials, roles and values of forests. The Strategy recognises the role that forestry can play in responding proactively and effectively to climate change, contributing to mitigation and adaptation activities. It aims to streamline the State administration system for forestry efficiently and effectively.

In pursuit of the general objectives, the Strategy follows specific economic, social, and environmental objectives. The Strategy sets specific targets for these objectives and sets out a more general vision to 2050.

The Strategy also provides future direction for development in specific fields, namely:
  • Forestry planning;
  • Forest management, protection and conservation of forest biodiversity and ecosystem services;
  • Forest development;
  • Forest use.

Notably, climate considerations are incorporated into forestry planning and forest development;

In addition, direction for future development is given by regions. The potential of wave breaking protection forests, coastal line erosion prevention protection forests and protection of other construction works for climate change responses is recognised for the Mekong River Delta region.

The Strategy recommends different solutions for these tasks. Such are:
  • Different mechanisms and policies;
  • Awareness raising communication;
  • Development, application of science, technologies and forestry promotion;
  • Human resource development;
  • Building forestry infrastructure, forestry industry and logistics services in a synchronous and modern matter;
  • Organisation of production and business;
  • Organisation and management of the sector;
  • International cooperation;
  • Monitoring and Evaluation.

Climate considerations are mainstreamed into scientific research and technological development; human resource development; international cooperations. 

The Strategy also delineates the different funding sources for the strategy implementation and puts forward institutional mandates.
Document Title: Decision no. 523/QD-TTg on approving the Viet Nam’s Forestry Development Strategy in the 2021-2030 period, with a vision to 2050

Four strategic axes of policy action are identified: 1) Climate-resilient food and landscapes: Agriculture, food security, forestry and natural resources (including water, biodiversity and wildlife), 2) Low emissions and resilient economy: Energy, transport, infrastructure and the key economic sectors of tourism and financial services, 3) Climate-resilient people: Health, education, equitable social development and human settlements, and 4) Climate-aware Integrated Coastal Zone Management.

Family Name: Summary of sector-specific low-carbon roadmaps
Family Summary:
"The outcomes of the sectoral roadmaps created over the previous year were summarized in a report published by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment. It demonstrates:

- With current or emerging technology, the government's objective of a carbon-neutral Finland by 2035 is feasible for industry and other sectors, but would require a supportive investment climate;

- The reduction of sectoral greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is mostly dependent on electrification, clean energy, and RDI investments. The availability of professionals, a transparent and predictable working environment, RDI investments, and easy regulation are essential prerequisites for the implementation of the roadmaps. Targeting RDI investments will shape future trends, making it one of the key concerns for building a low-carbon society.

Technologies for low-emission energy production, material and energy efficiency, alternative propulsion technologies (biofuels, hydrogen, electrification), waste heat recovery, and carbon capture, usage, and storage are among the technological solutions that are featured."

Family Name: Long-Term Climate Strategy, 2021
Family Summary:
This document aims to outline the path to reach net zero emissions by 2050, a goal decided by the Federal Council on August 28, 2019. The strategic principles set out in this document are as following:

  1. Switzerland will take advantage of the opportunities presented by a systematic transition to net zero.

  2. Switzerland will assume its climate policy responsibility.

  3. Priority will be given to reducing domestic emissions.

  4. Emissions will be reduced across entire value chains.

  5. All energy sources will be used effectively taking account of their optimal usage potential.

  6. The Swiss Confederation and the cantons will gear their planning activities to net zero in all climate- relevant areas.

  7. The transition to net zero will be carried out in a socially acceptable way.

  8. The transition to net zero will be achieved in an economically viable way.

  9. The transition to net zero will also improve environmental quality.

  10. The Long-Term Climate Strategy is based on openness to all types of technology.

Family Name: National Guidance on Voluntary Carbon Market Mechanisms
Family Summary:
The National Guidance on Voluntary Carbon Market Mechanisms includes provisions related to the institutional arrangement in the carbon market in Malaysia, specifically on the roles and responsibilities of project participants and the ministry in charge of climate change. The guidance sets out the technical requirements for a carbon project and requirements for project registration and reporting. The guidance also provides a short description and status of Malaysia's domestic emissions trading scheme.

Responsibilities of the carbon project developer

Project participants shall report the following to the Ministry in charge of climate change (Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability of Malaysia) and National Steering Committee on Climate Change (NSCCC):

a) Information on the carbon project;

b) The scope of the activity and the crediting periods;

c) The project boundary;

d) The methodology used and baselines developed;

e) Policy guidance applied to achieve the emission reductions; and

f) Annual reporting of units generated, sold, retired and cancelled.

For forestry projects, a project developer shall report the above to the National Steering Committee on REDD Plus (NSC REDD Plus)

Responsibilities of the Ministry in charge of climate change (Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability of Malaysia)

a) Host the Secretariat to the National Steering Committee on Climate Change (NSCCC) or any specific committee established under the NSCCC;

b) Provide guidance on carbon markets and propose mechanisms for domestic carbon markets as appropriate;

c) Maintain a registry to track all carbon projects;

d) Verify that no double counting occurs when reporting on nationally determined contribution (NDC) progress and achievement;

e) Undertake corresponding adjustments consistent with the decisions of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) on Article 6 of the Paris Agreement;

f) Report to UNFCCC on Malaysia’s participation in market mechanisms under the UNFCCC and voluntary carbon market;

g) Maintain Malaysia’s NDC in accordance with Article 4 paragraph 2 of Paris Agreement and decision 4/CMA.1 under the UNFCCC;

h) Ensure Malaysia’s participation in the voluntary carbon markets contributes to the implementation of Malaysia’s NDC and long-term low GHG emission development strategy;

i) Any other requirements agreed under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

Technical requirements of a carbon project

Activity design

  • The mitigation activity must

a) deliver real, measurable and long-term benefits related to climate;

b) minimise the risk of reversals and displacements of emission reductions, and where such reversals occur, ensure that they are fully addressed;

c) avoid negative environmental and social impacts;

d) avoid double financing;

e) establish a robust accounting system

  • In developing a carbon project, project developer/proponent must undergo stakeholder consultations including with local communities and indigenous peoples
  • There must be a transfer of technology, the applied technology must be environmentally sound and applicable for local environment
  • The mitigation activity must also 1) set a baseline 2) be additional 3) be monitored and 4) be quantifiable.

In addition to activity design, the national guidance also sets out the key requirements for carbon accounting, risks and reversal, corresponding adjustments, validation and verification, monitoring, issuance and renewal (Section 4.3 of the Guidance), as well as guidance on project registration and reporting (Section 5).
Document Title: National Guidance on Voluntary Carbon Market Mechanisms

Family Name: Economic and Social Development Plan - PDES 2021-2025
Family Summary:
• This document sets the government's development vision over the period 2021-2025. Under its 8th goal, the plan aims to: 8.1. Strengthen the comprehensive and sustainable management of forests as a strategic resource, promoting the protection of areas with a forestry vocation.
  • 8.2.Promote mitigation, adaptation and monitoring actions for climate change, with effective response measures to its impacts in harmony and balance with mother earth.
  • 8.3.Promote life systems with a healthy, protected and balanced environment in harmony with Mother Earth.
  • 8.4. Promote the system of protected areas, wetlands, bofedales, as part of the country's natural heritage.
  • 8.5. Strengthen the integrated management of surface and groundwater resources to achieve water security.


The plan also seeks to guarantee food security and sovereignty, with a specific focus on indigenous populations. It promotes productive capacities and potentialities, under comprehensive management of basins (water), air, soil, forest resources, flora, fauna, risk management and adaptation to climate change based on the formulation of a Plan with a Comprehensive Management approach of their Territories.

The plan further calls for an increase in renewable energy capacity.

Family Name: National Climate Change Response Strategy 2021 – 2026
Family Summary:
The overall the objective of the Strategy is to enhance the national resilience to the adverse impacts of climate change and enable the country to pursue low-emission development pathways to achieve sustainable development. The specific objectives of the NCCRS are to: - i) Enhance mainstreaming of climate change issues into national sector and local government development plans and budgets; ii). Facilitate implementation and monitoring of the Tanzania’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC); iii) Align climate change interventions with the national development agenda of industrialised economy; iv) Devise and implement strategic adaptation and mitigation measures in line with the national circumstances, requirements of climate change related multilateral environmental agreements, sustainable development goals (SDGs) and related bilateral and regional agreements; v) Enhance research, public awareness, education and capacity building on climate change issues; vi) Enhance coordination and institutional capacity, including provision of climate services and implementation of the national framework for climate services; vii) Facilitate mobilisation of sustainable and adequate finance and technologies to support climate change adaptation and mitigation interventions; viii) Promote and facilitate transfer of climate-smart technologies to support climate change adaptation and mitigation; ix) Promote gender-responsive climate change adaptation and mitigation interventions; and x) Promote inclusive engagement of stakeholders, including community, media, civil society organisations and private sector in designing, implementing and monitoring sustainable climate change adaptation and mitigation interventions.

It provides strategic interventions and action plan for climate change adaptation, climate change mitigations, disaster risk management and climate finance, among other issues.
Document Title: National Climate Change Response Strategy

Family Name: Net Zero Roadmap for the Singapore Public Sector
Family Summary: As Singapore has committed to achieve net zero emissions by 2050, the public sector has taken the lead by committing to achieve net zero emissions earlier around 2045, after peaking emissions around 2025, in this Roadmap. The public sector will reduce emissions from its operations; replace its current energy source with lower-carbon alterantives and remove carbon by exploring new technologies. Actions include designing energy-efficient infrastructure; using alternative using cars and buses running on cleaner energy; deploying solar energy; and exploring low-carbon electricity imports.This Roadmap arises from the Singapore Public Sector's membership in the Net Zero Government Initiative. Participating countries commit to achieving net zero emission from national government operations no later than 2050, and develop a roadmap that outlines the pathway for achieving the net zero commitment.
Document Title: Net Zero Roadmap for the Singapore Public Sector

Family Name: Strategic Plan of the Common Agricultural Policy of the Republic of Croatia 2023 - 2027
Family Summary: This Strategic Plan of the Common Agricultural Policy both recognises climate change as a major threat to agriculture in Croatia, and the agricultural sector as a major source of climate mitigation potential. The plan contains a wide range of measures to reduce emissions, enhance carbon storage and increase climate resilience in the agricultural sector nationally, interfacing with government, industry and the public. Greenhouse gas emissions reduction is named a major area of action in the plan, with high prioritisation. The plan aims to increase the usage of renewable energy sources in agricultural developments, and optimise land use and plantings for carbon storage. It highlights the potential for significant expansion in biomass energy production. It also proposes major forest restoration, and capacity building including the creation of a national forest registry. A major adaptation measure in the plan is to increase the total area of artificially irrigated land, improving crop supply resilience.
Document Title: Strategic Plan of the Common Agricultural Policy of the Republic of Croatia 2023 - 2027

Family Name: Climate Programme
Family Summary:
The Climate Act sets a target for Denmark to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 70 per cent in 2030 compared to 1990 levels. In the longer term, Denmark must be a climate-neutral society by 2050 at the latest. Each year, the Minister for Climate, Energy and Utilities must prepare a climate programme for the Danish Parliament, in which the minister must give his or her assessment of whether it can be demonstrated that the national climate targets will be achieved. The assessment of whether it is possible to demonstrate that the targets of the Climate Act will be achieved is based on an overall assessment of the short- and long-term effects of initiatives, where for some initiatives it will be possible to estimate a specific reduction effect. For other initiatives, an assessment of the expected reduction effect is made based on professional assumptions.

In accordance with the Climate Act, the Climate Council assessed the government's climate action in February 2021. The Climate Council assessed that the government had not demonstrated that the 70% target for 2030 would be achieved, in particular due to a lack of concrete climate action. Against this background, the Climate Council recommended, among other things, that the government present a roadmap for achieving the 70% target. With Climate Programme 2021, for instance, the government is presenting a comprehensive roadmap for achieving the 70% target in 2030, which demonstrates that the climate targets will be achieved. The roadmap states that by 2025 at the latest, the government will have presented proposals to ensure that the review is revisited all sectors and that we can make the necessary decisions towards 2025 to meet the 70% target. The roadmap is based on analyses by the Danish Energy Agency and relevant ministries of implementation speeds, scenarios, barriers, costs and maturity assessments of the individual technologies. The roadmap ensures that the necessary decisions can be made before it is too late, but also that decisions are not made too early in relation to the maturity of the technologies.
Document Title: Climate Programme 2022

Family Name: Agricultural Climate Solutions – On-Farm Climate Action Fund
Family Summary:
The objective of the fund is to support farmers in adopting beneficial management practices (BMPs) that store carbon and reduce greenhouse gases, specifically in the areas of:

  1. nitrogen management
  2. cover cropping
  3. rotational grazing practices

These practices also provide other environmental benefits such as improved biodiversity and soil health.

Other activities to support the adoption of beneficial management practices, such as outreach, education and training are offered.
Document Title: Agricultural Climate Solutions – On-Farm Climate Action Fund

Family Name: Natural Climate Solutions Fund
Family Summary:
To address climate change and biodiversity loss, the Government of Canada has established the Natural Climate Solutions Fund, which will invest over $5 billion from 2021 to 2031. This initiative consists of three distinct, but related, programs:

•   2 Billion Trees Program led by Natural Resources Canada ($3.19 billion): However, as announced in the Federal Fall Budget of 2025, the Government of Canada will wind down the 2 Billion Trees (2BT) program. While existing agreements will be honoured, the program is no longer accepting applications.

  • Nature Smart Climate Solutions led by Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) ($1.4 billion). Within this fund, up to $76.9 million has been set aside for Indigenous-led Natural Climate Solutions, to provide targeted support to Indigenous Nations, communities and organizations to engage as leaders in natural climate solutions.
  • Agricultural Climate Solutions led by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada ($885 million)

The objectives are to:

  • Avoid GHG emissions by halting or reducing the conversion of carbon rich ecosystems to another less carbon rich ecosystem (e.g. from a forest/grassland/wetland to cropland or an urban development)
  • Restore carbon storage and biodiversity in converted or degraded ecosystems
  • Reduce GHG emissions caused by natural resource use, including by implementing new forest harvesting management practices

Family Name: Natural Climate Solutions Fund
Family Summary:
To address climate change and biodiversity loss, the Government of Canada has established the Natural Climate Solutions Fund, which will invest over $5 billion from 2021 to 2031. This initiative consists of three distinct, but related, programs:

•   2 Billion Trees Program led by Natural Resources Canada ($3.19 billion): However, as announced in the Federal Fall Budget of 2025, the Government of Canada will wind down the 2 Billion Trees (2BT) program. While existing agreements will be honoured, the program is no longer accepting applications.

  • Nature Smart Climate Solutions led by Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) ($1.4 billion). Within this fund, up to $76.9 million has been set aside for Indigenous-led Natural Climate Solutions, to provide targeted support to Indigenous Nations, communities and organizations to engage as leaders in natural climate solutions.
  • Agricultural Climate Solutions led by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada ($885 million)

The objectives are to:

  • Avoid GHG emissions by halting or reducing the conversion of carbon rich ecosystems to another less carbon rich ecosystem (e.g. from a forest/grassland/wetland to cropland or an urban development)
  • Restore carbon storage and biodiversity in converted or degraded ecosystems
  • Reduce GHG emissions caused by natural resource use, including by implementing new forest harvesting management practices
  • Develop policies, programs or tools with key actors in priority sectors, and implement them to reduce GHG emissions and improve biodiversity
  • Measure and report on GHG outcomes from natural climate solutions
  • Provide biodiversity and human well-being co-benefits
  • Advance the federal commitment to reconciliation with Indigenous people
  • Advance science and knowledge on natural climate solutions in Canada
Document Title: 2 Billion Trees Program

Family Name: Italy's Long-Term Strategy for Reducing Greenhouse Gas Emissions
Family Summary: The long-term Italian strategy on reducing emissions of greenhouse gases is a national multisectoral strategy of Italy for the period up to 2050. Its main objective is to identify, in compliance with the Paris Agreement, possible paths to reach, by 2050, a condition of climate neutrality, in which the residual greenhouse gas emissions are offset by the absorption of CO2 and from the possible use of forms of geological storage and reuse of CO2.
Document Title: Italy's long-term strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions ( Strategia Italiana di Lungo Termine sulla Riduzione delle Emissioni dei Gas a Effetto Serra)

Family Name: Natural Infrastructure Fund
Family Summary:
Announced in June 2021, the $200 million Natural Infrastructure Fund supports projects that use natural or hybrid approaches to protect the natural environment, support healthy and resilient communities, and contribute to economic growth and jobs.

The Natural Infrastructure Fund will bring real benefits to communities across Canada, including:

  • Increasing climate change resilience
  • Mitigating carbon emissions
  • Improving the environment, such as contributing to cleaner air and water
  • Protecting and preserving biodiversity and wildlife habitats
  • Promoting people's access to nature

A minimum of 10% of the overall program envelope will be allocated to Indigenous-led projects.
Document Title: Natural Infrastructure Fund

Family Name: Clean Fuels Fund
Family Summary:
Budget 2021 invested $1.5 billion over five years to establish a Clean Fuels Fund to de-risk the capital investment required to build new or expand existing clean fuel production facilities (including facility conversions). Support was also available for feasibility and front-end engineering and design (FEED) studies, and the establishment of biomass supply chains to improve logistics for the collection, supply, and distribution of biomass materials (e.g., forest residues, municipal solid waste, and agriculture crop residues) as a feedstock in clean fuel production facilities. Resources were also available to address gaps and misalignment in codes, standards and regulations related to the production, distribution and end-use of clean fuels.

Budget 2024 announced the retooling of the Clean Fuels Fund and its extension to March 31, 2030. Support is available to de-risk capital investments and studies that expand Canada’s clean fuel production capacity, and to address gaps and misalignment in codes, standards and regulations. The program has shifted to a continuous intake process to deliver funding faster and will streamline negotiations and decision-making processes to expedite delivery.
Document Title: Clean Fuels Fund

Family Name: First national adaption plan for climate change: Republic of South Sudan
Family Summary:
This document, South Sudan’s first NAP for climate change, is a landmark achievement in the country’s response to climate change. The first NAP represents an important milestone in establishing a coordinated approach to building adaptive capacity and resilience to better manage the challenges the country faces, including changing environmental conditions associated with climate change and global warming. The first NAP also follows guidelines introduced by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in 2019.
The vision of the NAP is to mainstream adaptation planning within South Sudan’s development planning across different government line ministries and climate resilient communities. This will ensure climate-centric development for long term resilience and interruption of the poverty cycle. The mandate of the NAP is to build leadership and ensure stakeholder participation to fulfill South Sudan’s commitment to the UNFCCC and to operationalize climate change adaptation at all levels. The NAP will play a number of key roles for South Sudan, including the following:

Provide a roadmap of the steps needed to mainstream climate change adaptation into planning and budgeting at national, state and local levels.
Identify actions that are needed to create enabling conditions for scaled up access to international climate finance from both public and private sources.
Provide a baseline and starting point for climate change adaptation in South Sudan by consolidating all relevant information on the physical processes and impacts of climate change to establish a common understanding for all stakeholders.
Provide a common and coherent articulation of adaptation priorities to guide and coordinate all stakeholders, including government agencies, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), development partners, civil society organizations and the private sector, along the same pathway to a resilient and climate-adapted South Sudan. This includes providing a framework for determining and fulfilling South Sudan’s international commitments with respect to climate change adaptation.
Document Title: First national adaption plan for climate change: Republic of South Sudan

Family Name: Tree Planting Plan
Family Summary: This plan sets out the target to plant 1 billion trees by 2025. From This initiative helps to reduce environmental degradation and restore biodiversity. Between 2021-2023, Viet Nam planted about 770 million trees, already exceeding its plan by 121%.
Document Title: Decision 524/QD-TT-g approving the Project "Planting One Billion Trees from 2021-2025"

Family Name: 10-year development plan (2020/21-2029/30)
Family Summary: This plan sets the government's development vision over the decade 2020-2030. It is based on ten pillars. Pillar six is to build a climate resilient, green economy.  It seeks to increase basin development efforts to fight land degradation and to reduce pollutions, improve productivity and reduce GHG emissions, increase forest protection and development, increase production of electricity from renewable sources for domestic use and for export, and focus on modern and energy saving technologies.
Document Title: 10-year development plan (2020/21-2029/30)

Family Name: CONPES 4021 - National Policy for the Control of Deforestation and Sustainable Management of Forests
Family Summary:
This CONPES document provides policy guidelines to counteract deforestation and promote sustainable forest management. Through the analysis of the causes that affect the processes of land use change and loss of natural forest, it identifies the actions that the national government should develop in coordination with the sectors, communities and other actors so that, based on the recognition of the particularities and needs of the territories, this problem can be controlled and at the same time the conservation and sustainable management of forests can be promoted.

In particular, four strategic lines are established to lead the country to achieve the goal of zero net deforestation by 2030: (i) integrate strategies for the sustainable use of forests to improve the quality of life and the local economy of communities; (ii) articulate cross-sectoral actions that allow the national government to work together to manage forests and address territorial conflicts; (iii) promote prevention strategies and territorial control to reduce illegal dynamics, and (iv) strengthen the management of information for decision-making.

This policy focuses on actions foreseen under the Integrated Strategy for the Control of Deforestation and Forest Management (EICD).
Document Title: CONPES 4021 - National Policy for the Control of Deforestation and Sustainable Management of Forests (POLÍTICA NACIONAL PARA EL CONTROL DE LA DEFORESTACIÓN Y LA GESTIÓN SOSTENIBLE DE LOS BOSQUES)

Family Name: Climate Action Plan 2020
Family Summary: In line with the Climate Act, the government must publish a climate action plan in 2020. Going forward, the government must present a comprehensive climate action plan every five years with a ten-year target. This is to ensure ongoing progress towards climate neutrality in 2050. The first comprehensive climate action plan consists of the sector strategies agreed with the Folketing, initiated initiatives to involve business and civil society, and indicators for the various sectors. The sector strategies, the decision of the Funen Power Plant to stop coal, the agreement on green tax reform, and the finance law agreements for 2020 and 2021 bring the total expected reduction to 7.2 million tonnes in 2030. This corresponds to one third of the necessary reductions up to 2030.
Document Title: Climate Action Plan 2020

Collection Summary: he Effort Sharing Regulation (ESR) is an EU law that sets binding annual greenhouse gas emission targets for each member state in sectors not covered by the EU Emissions Trading System — like transport, buildings, agriculture, and waste. Its goal is to ensure a fair contribution from all countries toward the EU’s overall climate targets.
Family Name: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/2126 on setting out the annual emission allocations of the Member States for the period from 2021 to 2030 pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2018/842
Family Summary:
Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/2126, adopted on 16 December 2020, establishes the annual greenhouse gas emission allocations (AEAs) for each EU Member State for the period 2021–2030 under the Effort Sharing Regulation (ESR). It defines the 2005 baseline emissions for every Member State and specifies the annual emission limits each country must respect throughout the decade. The Decision also sets out the total quantities that can be used for compliance through flexibility mechanisms, such as limited use of ETS allowances or land-use credits. Three annexes provide detailed data: Annex I lists the 2005 baseline emissions, Annex II gives the annual emission allocations for each year from 2021 to 2030, and Annex III sets out the total quantities available under flexibility provisions.

Since its adoption, the Decision has been amended several times to update the data and reflect changes in EU climate policy. Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1319 revised the AEAs for 2023–2030 to align with the higher climate ambition introduced by the revised Effort Sharing Regulation. Implementing Decision (EU) 2024/1884 introduced further updates and corrections to the national allocations, ensuring consistency with the most recent emissions data. Finally, Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/1405 made additional adjustments, likely to incorporate updated figures or methodological improvements. Together, these amendments ensure that Member States’ emission limits remain accurate and in line with the evolving EU legislative framework and climate targets.
Document Title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/1405 amending Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/2126 as regards the total quantities of cancelled EU ETS allowances that may be taken into account for certain Member States’ compliance under Regulation (EU) 2018/842

Family Name: National Agroforestry Policy
Family Summary: Belize's National Agroforestry Policy notes climate change as a key threat to agricultural systems nationally, through drought, flooding and other extreme weather, and underscores the importance of developing agroforestry techniques and practice to enhance climate resilience and long-term sustainability. It aims to contribute to sustainable development goals on poverty, hunger, gender equality, climate action and biodiversity. The policy promotes agroforestry as a convenient synergy with REDD+ efforts, integrating trees and shrubs into crop and pasture systems, enhancing overall carbon storage and landscape resilience. It notes that some existing agroforestry techniques are unsustainable, leading to ecosystem degradation, and promotes measures to implement crop rotation and better manage fallow land. It aims to enhance investment and awareness in agroforestry best-practice across the country.
Document Title: National Agroforestry Policy

Family Name: Agreement on the future of oil and gas extraction in the North Sea (2020)
Family Summary:
The Government and a broad majority in the Danish Parliament decided to allocate DKK 200 million in 2021-22 for development projects for CO2 storage in the North Sea. This was based on the rationale that the North Sea holds great potential for storing CO2 in former oil and gas reservoirs and can support Denmark's green transition and path towards the 70% reduction target in 2030 and climate neutrality by 2050. At the same time, CCS projects have the potential to support local employment in the same areas as the oil and gas sector is based.

The agreement also cancels the 8th tender round and sets an end date for oil and gas extraction in the North Sea in 2050, to achieve the Paris Agreement's goal of limiting the global temperature increase to 1.5 degrees and fulfill Denmark's obligation to act on behalf of future generations.
Document Title: Agreement on the future of oil and gas extraction in the North Sea (2020)

Family Name: 2050 carbon neutral strategy
Family Summary: The 2050 carbon neutral strategy is South Korea's UN-LEDS. It outlines five key elements to achieve carbon neutrality: Expanding the use of clean power and hydrogen across all sectors; Improving energy efficiency to a significant level; Commercial deployment of carbon removal and other future technologies; Scaling up the circular economy to improve industrial sustainability; Enhancing carbon sinks. It further sets sectoral decarbonisation orientations.
Document Title: 2050 carbon neutral strategy

Family Name: Energy White Paper
Family Summary:
In December 2020 the UK Secretary for Business, Energy, and Industrial Strategy issued an Energy White Paper entitled "Powering our Net Zero Future". The aim of the White Paper is to transform energy, support a green recovery from the COVID19 crisis and create a fair deal for consumers. The government estimates that the measures set out in the White Paper could reduce emissions across power, industry and buildings by up to 230MtCO2e in the period to 2032, as well as creating thousands of jobs.

Among the measures proposed, the paper includes further detail on previous policies regarding a ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2030, financial support for an extra 40 gigawatts (40GW) of new offshore wind, and £3bn in funding for home energy improvements. The paper also envisages experimentation with a number of other mechanisms to keep energy affordable for consumers.

One of the key elements of the paper is the provision of details on the establishment of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme, which will include a cap on emissions that is 5% lower than under the previous EU Emissions Trading Scheme and will be lowered further over time to ensure a net zero trajectory. 

The paper also sets out Government plans for nuclear energy, including the intention to create a commercially viable nuclear fusion plant by 2040. Additional funding is also intended to be made available for the development of new carbon capture and storage technologies.
Document Title: Energy White Paper

Family Name: Vision and Development Strategy of Slovakia until 2030
Family Summary:
This long-term sustainable development strategy, approved by Government Resolution No. 41 of 20 January 2021, also fulfils the role of the National Strategy for Regional Development of the Slovak Republic. It thus integrates sectoral priorities and regional and territorial development priorities. It is based on four principles: sustainability, the priority of quality of life over economic growth, efficiency based on synergies, and the integration of policies and their instruments.

In terms of environmental objectives, Slovakia 2030 is to ensure the protection, restoration and enhancement of natural resources, including ensuring the stability and health of ecosystems and their services, and the reflection of adaptation and mitigation measures to the adverse effects of climate change in all departmental strategic documents and municipal and regional development documents as an overriding public interest (e.g. in transport planning, energy, spatial planning, spatial planning, water management, land management, forestry, sustainable tourism, overall care of the countryside, etc.).
Document Title: Resolution 41/2021 approving the Vision and Development Strategy

It notably assesses how to reduce the adverse impacts from climate change, decarbonise shipping and develop a low-emission economy.
Document Title: Blue Economy Development Framework for Indonesia’s Economic Transformation

Family Name: Notification S.O. 4259(E) creating the Apex Committee for Implementation of Paris Agreement
Family Summary:
This document from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change creates the Apex Committee for Implementation of Paris Agreement (AIPA). It further sets its composition and missions. 

This Committee is notably tasked to develop policies and programmes, if required, to make India’s domestic climate actions compliant with its international obligation, and to function as a National Authority to regulate carbon markets in India, under Article 6.2, Article 6.4 and Article 6.8 of the Paris Agreement in the post-2020 period;

Family Name: 2030 Agriculture and Fisheries Development Plan
Family Summary: The aim of this Development Plan(PõKa 2030) is to contribute to the increase in competitiveness of these areas, food security, sustainable development of rural and coastal areas, good plant and animal health, improvement of soil condition, food safety and preservation of a clean environment and species diversity. In this way, the PõKa 2030 creates the prerequisites for increasing added value in these areas, taking into account the bioeconomy, sustainable development and environmental goals, and creates opportunities for cross-sectoral cooperation. Family Name: Guidelines for Sustainable Use of Peat Resources for 2020-2030
Family Summary: The Guidelines for Sustainable Use of Peat Resources 2020-2030 (adopted by CoM Order 696/2020 on 24 November 2020) covers main aspects of sustainability of the peat extraction and production. In order to ensure the sustainable development of the peat industry, the main directions of action have been identified: inventory of peat deposits and ensuring sustainable management and use of peat resources in the national economy; improvement of the legal framework for the use of bogs and building institutional capacity; improvement of the availability of information and promoting scientific research and innovative solutions for peat extraction and development and GHG emission accounting. For every direction of action specific measures to be performed, results to be achieved and responsible institutions are determined.
Document Title: Order 696/2020 on Guidelines for Sustainable Use of Peat Resources for 2020-2030

Family Name: Greening Government Strategy
Family Summary:
This strategy aims at reducing GHG emissions and increase the resilience of Canada's federal government. It builds on the Federal Sustainable Development Strategy. It seeks to transition to net-zero carbon and climate-resilient operations, while also reducing environmental impacts beyond carbon, including on waste, water and biodiversity.The strategy notably sets goals with regard to low-carbon transport and real property.

The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat’s Centre for Greening Government operates a Low-carbon Fuel Procurement Program (LCFPP) within the Greening Government Fund. The LCFPP has $134.9 million in funding over eight years (fiscal years 2023–24 to 2030–31) to support the purchase of low-carbon-intensity liquid fuels for federal air and marine fleet operations and in 2024, the program was expanded to include the procurement of CDR services.
Document Title: Greening Government Strategy

Family Name: The Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading Scheme Order 2020 (S.I. 1265/2020)
Family Summary:
This order established a new UK emissions trading regime as the successor to the EU Emissions Trading Scheme following the UK's Withdrawal from the European Union. The scheme applies to greenhouse gas emissions from power and heat generations, energy intensive industries, and aviation.The order provides details on the rules governing the issuance and surrender of "allowances" equivalent to emissions falling within the scope of the sceheme. A number of derogations from the general rules are created for hospitals and small and ultra-small emitters. A modified version of the EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification scheme is also mandated under the legislation.The order also describes the different agencies responsible for the regulation of the scheme across the UK and provides for enforcement of the scheme and sets out the penalty regime for non-compliance.The first UKA auction took place in May 2021.

The Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading Scheme (Amendment) (No. 2) Order 2024 (S.I. 2024/1366) introduces key updates to the primary 2020 UK ETS Order (S.I. 2020/1265) to align the UK Emissions Trading Scheme with Net Zero targets:

  • Tighter Emissions Cap: Significantly lowers the overall scheme cap and the yearly base allowances from 2024 through 2030 to align carbon budgets with net-zero trajectories.
  • Flexible Reserve: Establishes a new "flexible reserve" pool of allowances to manage unallocated or returned free allowances and support future market stability mechanisms.
  • Aviation Scope Expansion: Expands aviation compliance obligations
Document Title: The Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading Scheme Order 2020

Family Name: Long-term decarbonisation Strategy. Strategy for a modern, competitive and climate neutral Spanish economy by 2050
Family Summary:
This Spanish long-term strategy outlines the roadmap for Spain to achieve climate neutrality by 2050, aligning with the European Union's commitment under the European Green Deal and the Paris Agreement. Recognising Spain's vulnerability to climate change, the strategy aims to transform the economy to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, with intermediate milestones in 2030 and 2040. It emphasises leveraging the opportunities presented by this transition for economic modernisation and increased competitiveness, while ensuring a socially just and inclusive process that leaves no one behind.
The strategy is built on the principle of technological neutrality, encouraging the development of cost-effective decarbonisation solutions across all sectors. It seeks to provide long-term signals to investors and stakeholders, fostering innovation, job creation, and strengthening Spain's research and development capabilities. This plan builds upon existing frameworks like the National Integrated Energy and Climate Plan (PNIEC) and emphasises the importance of a just transition, addressing energy poverty, and adapting to the impacts of climate change. The strategy also recognises the need to accelerate the ecological transition as part of the post-COVID-19 recovery efforts.
Document Title: Long-term decarbonisation Strategy. Strategy for a modern, competitive and climate neutral Spanish economy by 2050

Family Name: Agricultural Transition Plan
Family Summary: The Agricultural Transition Plan is the UK government’s plan for restructuring agricultural policy in England from 2021-2028 following Brexit and the end of EU subsidies. It is designed to modernise the agricultural sector, emphasising environmental stewardship and resilience in the face of climate change and the transition from direct subsidies to farmers. The plan seeks to gradually phase out the Basic Payment Scheme (BPS), replacing it with new initiatives focused on environmental sustainability, productivity, and animal welfare. The proposals in the plan aim to support farmers in adapting to new business models while addressing climate change and biodiversity challenges.
Document Title: Agricultural Transition Plan

Family Name: Strategy for Green Public Procurement - Action Plan for Green Public Procurement 2020-2030
Family Summary:
This Strategy was launched with the aim of public procurement helping to achieve the goal of a 70 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. The strategy is based on three tracks, all of which focus on procurement areas in the public sector that currently have a significant climate footprint, including:

  1. An implementation track that creates green action now,
  2. a development path that creates long-term green action towards 2030,
  3. and a track related to green knowledge and green tools.

Under these three tracks, the strategy presents initiatives that are already being launched, as well as initiatives with a longer development horizon. The initiatives range widely across both stages of the procurement process and procurement areas.

For instance, 60 percent of the food must be organic, that food waste from canteen operations be combated, and that a meat-free alternative is always offered. Climate compensation for all government flights is paid annually to the Climate Forest Fund, to ensure that new forests are planted in Denmark.

For longer-term initiatives, work has been initiated to draw up a plan for a shift to emission-free cars in the state, municipalities and regions, so that the public car fleet can be emission-free in 2030. The Secretariat for Green Procurement in the Danish Environmental Protection Agency is being strengthened and made the main entry point for guidance, advice and knowledge sharing and dissemination regarding green public procurement.
Document Title: Strategy for Green Public Procurement - Action Plan for Green Public Procurement 2020-2030

Family Name: Longship – Carbon capture and storage (Meld. St. 33 2019-2020)
Family Summary:
The Norwegian Government has decided to call the Norwegian project on carbon capture, transport and storage Longship, in Norwegian ‘Langskip’, as the characteristic shape, and flexible, supple construction of the Vikings’ longships made them one of the greatest innovations and most ground-breaking ship-building technologies of their day. LLike those who built the longships, the Norwegians also aim to take their technology out into the world, but only by peaceful means. Longship will bring Norway to the forefront of the development of a technology that could prove decisive in achieving our climate targets.

This policy document includes a section on how carbon capture and storage (CCS) can be made successful, which includes market development; having other countries support CCS; research, development and demonstration; and government contribution to developing technology. It also includes a development plan for the Northern Lights CCS project, which is a subsea reservoir for CCS.
Document Title: Longship – Carbon capture and storage (Meld. St. 33 2019-2020)

Collection Name: Law 7/2021 on climate change and energy transition [Spain]
Collection Summary:
Enacted in 2021, this law establishes Spain's legal framework for achieving climate neutrality by 2050, aligning with the Paris Agreement and Sustainable Development Goals. It mandates a 23% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 (compared to 1990 levels), alongside ambitious renewable energy targets, including 42% of final energy consumption from renewables and 74% renewable electricity generation by 2030. Energy efficiency measures aim for a 39.5% reduction in primary energy consumption within the same timeframe. The law also prohibits new hydrocarbon and radioactive mineral exploitation, requires emission-free transport systems in cities with populations exceeding 50,000, and emphasises sustainable urban mobility.

The legislation includes a national Just Transition Strategy to ensure equitable economic opportunities, particularly for vulnerable regions, while fostering adaptation and resilience to climate risks across critical sectors such as water, biodiversity, and health. It creates governance mechanisms like the Expert Committee on Climate Change and Energy Transition to monitor progress and updates to Spain's Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan (PNIEC). Projecting investments exceeding €200 billion by 2030, the law is expected to enhance Spain’s GDP by €16.5–25.7 billion annually and generate 250,000–350,000 new jobs. The focus on education, innovation, and public awareness underscores its commitment to a holistic and inclusive transition.

This collection represent a body of policies, strategies, and plans enacted under this law.
Family Name: Spanish Strategy for Science, Technology, and Innovation 2021-2027 (EECTI 2021-2027)
Family Summary: The Spanish Strategy for Science, Technology, and Innovation 2021-2027 (EECTI 2021-2027) serves as the foundational framework for strengthening and consolidating Spain's Science, Technology, and Innovation System (SECTI) over seven years. It aligns national RDI policies with the European Union's strategies, leveraging synergies to enhance scientific, technological, and industrial progress. Drafted during the COVID-19 pandemic, the strategy addresses pandemic-related challenges and underscores the critical role of science and innovation in socio-economic recovery and resilience. It adopts a phased approach: the first phase (2021–2023) focuses on reinforcing existing strengths, investing in healthcare RDI, ecological transition, and digitalisation, while the second phase (2024–2027) prioritises knowledge-driven economic growth and institutionalising RDI as a cornerstone of national development.The EECTI 2021-2027 identifies six thematic clusters essential for addressing Spain’s strategic priorities: health, inclusive society and creativity, societal security, digital and industrial advancements, climate and energy, and sustainable food systems. It integrates the objectives of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and EU programmes, particularly Horizon Europe. The strategy also emphasises enhancing investment in RDI, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration, and advancing technologies to mitigate demographic challenges and promote regional equity. Ultimately, the EECTI aims to position Spain as a leader in innovation, fostering high-quality employment and long-term socio-economic sustainability.
Document Title: Spanish Strategy for Science, Technology, and Innovation 2021-2027 (EECTI 2021-2027)

Family Name: Lebanon National Agriculture Strategy (NAS). 2020-2025.
Family Summary: Lebanon's National Agriculture Strategy (NAS). 2020-2025 recognises climate change as a major threat to the security of the agricultural sector, and names climate resilience among its five overarching pillars: restoring the livelihoods of producers; increasing agricultural production; enhancing efficiency of value chains; improving climate change adaptation and sustainable management of agrifood systems and natural resources; strengthening and enabling the institutional environment. Climate-related provisions include plans for significant afforestation, both for climate mitigation and to build landscape-level resilience, and the use of renewable energy in the agricultural sector where possible. The strategy also notes that more efficient water usage is a key element of agricultural adaptation to climate change, and promotes the adoption of modernised irrigation techniques.
Document Title: Lebanon National Agriculture Strategy (NAS). 2020-2025.

Family Name: President's Expanded Priority Program (PROPEP 2020-2023)
Family Summary: This document introduces a stimulus programme to combat the adverse effects of the COVID-19-induced economic crisis. It seeks to 1) intensify public investment, particularly in priority productive sectors with a view to accelerating the achievement of food self-sufficiency and in green sectors; 2) establish a Strategic Investment Fund; 3) initiate the formalisation of the economy; 4) simplify administrative procedures; 5) improve the business environment; and 6) lay the institutional foundations for strong and effective governance to support the private sector.The program notably allocates funds towards reforestation and sustainable forest management efforts, and the creation of green jobs. It aims to restore and ensure sustainable management of forest areas and degraded lands with a view to improving the livelihoods of local populations. It also contributes to better pollution management and the promotion of waste recovery channels capable of creating sustainable jobs, especially for young people. The envelope devoted to this axis represents an amount of MRU 961.9 million, or 4% of the overall funding.From this specific envelope, 350 million MRU will go toward the national reforestation program, including schools and public spaces. Further details on the allocation of this envelope are as follows:- Reinforcement of the national initiative of the great green wall for an envelope of 250 million MRU, or 26% of the financing of axis, allowing the realization of multipurpose gardens or Integrated Community Agricultural Farms,- Reduce pollution and improve the management and recovery of urban solid waste. for an overall envelope of MRU 361.9 million, i.e. 37.6% of the funding for the axis. This envelope will be intended for the ongoing program to clean up 33 municipalities in the interior of the country and its renewal for an additional year, as well as the development and introduction of a mercury-free extraction process for artisanal gold.
Document Title: President's Expanded Priority Program (PROPEP 2020-2023)

Family Name: National Strategy for Biological Diversity and its Action Plan 2012-2022 (Estrategia Nacional de Diversidad Biológica y su Plan de Acción 2012-2022)
Family Summary:
The National Strategy for Biological Diversity and its Action Plan 2012-2022, developed under Guatemala’s commitments to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), provides the national framework for conserving, valuing, and sustainably using biological diversity, while ensuring its integration into broader development and climate change policies. The strategy responds to accelerating biodiversity loss, deforestation, and ecosystem degradation, which undermine rural livelihoods, food security, and national economic sectors such as forestry, hydropower, and tourism. Recognising biodiversity as a foundation of national development and a critical instrument for climate change adaptation, it aligns with the Política Nacional de Diversidad Biológica and incorporates cross‑sectoral objectives that link environmental governance with poverty reduction and sustainable development.

The strategy is structured around five thematic axes: (i) knowledge and valuation of biodiversity, including scientific research and traditional practices; (ii) conservation and restoration, emphasising in situ and ex situ measures, ecosystem recovery, and community engagement; (iii) sustainable use, through productive systems and equitable benefit-sharing; (iv) biodiversity and climate change, promoting adaptive and mitigation strategies and financing mechanisms such as REDD+, payments for ecosystem services, and carbon markets; and (v) implementation and governance, which seeks to strengthen legal, institutional, and financial capacities. Specific lines of action focus on reducing deforestation and degradation to lower greenhouse gas emissions, securing ecosystem services related to water, food, and energy, and reducing socio‑environmental vulnerability. The plan establishes a monitoring and evaluation framework, with indicators to assess outcomes and to foster accountability across government ministries, local authorities, the Consejo Nacional de Áreas Protegidas (CONAP), civil society, indigenous organisations, and the private sector.
Document Title: National Policy on Biological Diversity - Government Agreement 220-2011 / National Strategy on Biological Diversity and its Action Plan 2012-2022 (Política Nacional de Diversidad Biológica - Acuerdo Gubernativo 220-2011 / Estrategia Nacioal de Diversidad Biológica y su Plan de Acción 2012-2022)

It requires Member States to prepare integrated national energy and climate plans (NECPs), report progress regularly, and ensures that the EU meets its climate, renewable energy, and energy efficiency targets. The Regulation also establishes mechanisms for reviewing data, assessing collective progress, and coordinating policies to achieve the EU’s long-term climate and energy objectives.
Family Name: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1208 on structure, format, submission processes and review of information reported by Member States pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2018/1999
Family Summary: Commission Implementing Regulation 2020/1208 sets out the detailed rules for how Member States must report information under Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 (the Governance of the Energy Union and Climate Action). Specifically, it defines the structure, format, submission processes, and review procedures for the reports and data that Member States provide to the Commission. It covers things like templates for progress reports and greenhouse‑gas inventories, timing and review cycles, and how the Commission and the European Environment Agency (EEA) conduct comprehensive reviews of the reported data. The amendments brought by Commission Implementing Regulation 2024/1281 improves reporting and review processes.

Family Name: Council of Ministers Resolution n.º 53/2020, last amended by Council of Ministers Resolution n.º 149/2024 approving the update of the NECP 2030
Family Summary:
The Resolution 53/2020 approves the National Energy and Climate Plans (NECP) 2030 and assigns to the newly renamed Commission for Climate Action the responsibility of overseeing and monitoring the implementation of the NECP 2030, as well as ensuring compliance with the established targets. It also establishes that the National System of Policies and Measures is responsible for the monitoring, evaluation, development of policies and measures, and projections of the NECP 2030.
Amid their goals, the resolutions aims to highlight the importance of meeting:
1 - National targets of the NECP 2030 for the year 2030, aligned with a carbon-neutral trajectory by 2050:
a) Reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 45% to 55%, compared to emissions recorded in 2005.
b) Incorporate 47% of energy from renewable sources into gross final energy consumption.
c) Reduce primary energy consumption by 35% to improve energy efficiency.
d) Achieve 15% electricity interconnections.
2 - Sector-specific greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets, compared to emissions recorded in 2005:
a) 70% in the services sector.
b) 35% in the residential sector.
c) 40% in the transport sector.
d) 11% in the agriculture sector.
e) 30% in the waste and wastewater sector.
In 2024, Resolution 49/2024 updated the NECP 2030 to reflect a a higher level of ambition than set in the initial version, in response to national and European developments and new legislation (i.e. Fit for 55 package).
The eight key objectives are: i) decarbonize the national economy; ii) prioritize energy efficiency; iii) increase renewable energy use and reduce energy dependence; iv) ensure supply security; v) promote sustainable mobility; vi) support sustainable agriculture and forestry, enhancing carbon sequestration; vii) develop an innovative and competitive industry; and viii) ensure a just, equitable, democratic, and cohesive transition.
Document Title: National Energy and Climate Plan 2030
